title: trust-tasks-rs-v0.21.21
body:
### Added

- **vtc/vetting/vetters/show**: A by-DID vetter status lookup ([#603](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/pull/603))

* feat(vtc/vetting/vetters/show): a by-DID vetter status lookup

  The vetter listing omits a vetter with no published profile and one whose
  grant was revoked in exactly the same way: both are simply absent. So an
  applicant whose vetter has gone quiet cannot tell which happened, and a
  vetter cannot check their own standing at all. The only way to find out
  today is to read the grant credential's status list, which needs the
  credential in hand.

  `vtc/vetting/vetters/show/0.1` answers by DID with one of `live`, `revoked`,
  `expired` or `none`, plus the grant id, the timestamp that ended or will end
  it, and — for a live grant — whether the vetter is listed, which is what
  separates "unlisted by choice" from "not a vetter".

  A new task rather than a `status` member on the listing response: adding a
  member to an existing response breaks consumers that reject unknown members,
  and the two answer different questions.

  `revoked` outranks `expired` where both hold, because withdrawal and lapse
  are different statements. `none` deliberately does not distinguish a
  non-member from a member who is not a vetter — the caller asked about
  vetting — and the revocation reason is not carried at all, including through
  `ext`.

  Rust, TypeScript and Go bindings regenerated.

title: build(deps)!: dtg-credentials 0.11
body:
Closes nothing; #1068 stays open.

Bumps the workspace `dtg-credentials` requirement from 0.9.1 to 0.11, which
crosses two releases: 0.10.0 was merged, versioned and never tagged, so
crates.io went straight from 0.9.1 to 0.11.0 and a consumer on 0.9.x takes both
sections at once. Step 2 of what #1068 still needs.

### What the bump crosses

Three compile-time changes, none of which changes a credential on the wire:

- `DTGCredentialError` is `#[non_exhaustive]` and gains nine variants across the
  two releases. **The workspace has no `match` on it at all**, so nothing needed
  a wildcard arm.
- `DTGCommon` gains a public `task_digest_multibase` field. **The workspace has
  no exhaustive `DTGCommon` struct literal**, as the upstream change predicted;
  every construction goes through a `new_*` constructor and `..Default::default()`.
- Three constructors are deprecated, not removed. They still compile, but CI's
  clippy runs `-D warnings`, so every call site moves.

### Call sites moved

All four are test fixtures — the workspace issues no VMC acknowledgement or VWC
in production code today.

| Site | From | To |
|---|---|---|
| `vtc-service/src/members/inbound_vmc.rs` (`pair`) | `new_member_vmc` | `new_member_vmc_for(&grant_wire, "did:key:zMember", …)` |
| `vtc-service/src/routes/relationships.rs` (`member_row`) | `new_member_vmc` | `new_member_vmc_for(&grant_json, did, …)` |
| `vtc-service/src/credentials/witness.rs` (`vwc_for`) | `new_vwc` | `new_vwc_for_session(…, &witness_session(), digest, …)` |
| `vtc-service/src/routes/members/personhood.rs` (`presentation_with_witness`) | `new_vwc` | `new_vwc_for_session(…, &witness_session(), digest, …)` |

The `_for` forms take the party the grant is expected to name, established
independently of the grant, and refuse a mismatch — so each site now passes the
member DID it already had rather than letting the constructor read one out of
the document it is meant to be checked against.

`new_vwc_for_session` reads **both** halves of the citation off the
`witness/session` document — `taskContext` from its `id`, `taskDigestMultibase`
from its task digest — so the two cannot disagree. Both test helpers therefore
gained a `witness_session()` fixture: the opening document, with `threadId`
equal to its own `id`, which is what the constructor requires and refuses
otherwise.

One consequence worth naming. `new_vwc_for_session` takes the edge digest as
REQUIRED, which the specification makes it, so it cannot produce the
"witness with no `digestMultibase`" case `personhood.rs` tests. That case is a
VWC predating the requirement, and the only honest way to hold one is to drop
the member from the wire form, which is how it would arrive — so the helper now
builds the credential and removes `credentialSubject.digestMultibase` for that
one case rather than asking the constructor for something it should refuse.

### One fixture the stricter checks refused

`vti-rooms-dtg`'s `an_expired_nomination_is_refused` built its "stale" nomination with
`validFrom` a minute ago and `validUntil` a **day** ago — a window that closes before it
opens. 0.10.0's `InvalidValidityWindow` caught it at construction.

The fixture was wrong, not the check. A credential whose window never opened is malformed,
not expired, so the test was asserting that `verify` refuses something — just not the thing
its name claims, and the refusal it was getting would have been the same for a credential
with no window at all. The window now opens two days ago and closes one day ago, so it is
an expiry the test can actually be about. `nomination()` gained a `valid_from` parameter so
every call site states both ends rather than one; passing only `validUntil` is exactly what
let this read as expired while being malformed.

No check was loosened. It was the only fixture any of 0.10.0's new refusals caught:
nothing else in the workspace nests past `MAX_JSON_DEPTH` or answers a grant that names
somebody else.

### `cites_task` on the verifier: not yet, and why

#1068's remaining item 3 asks whether `credentials::witness` should now pair a
presented VWC with its session document through `cites_task`. It should
eventually, but it is not a small addition and is deliberately not in this PR.

`cites_task(&self, document)` needs the `witness/session` document itself.
`resolve_binding` has the relationships keyspace and the presented credential
JSON, and neither the VTC nor the presentation carries that document:

- there is no wire slot for it — `extract_vp_claims` projects credentials, and
  a cited Trust Task document is not one;
- the VTC was not a party to the witnessing exchange. A VWC presented at a join
  names a *foreign* exchange by construction (`TaskContextBinding::ForeignExchange`
  is the honest case, not the suspicious one), so the VTC cannot have retained
  the document;
- even `credentials::task_context::resolve`, which does compare a credential's
  `taskContext` against the ceremony it was presented in, compares thread ids —
  it has no document to digest either, and Trust Task documents are not stored.

Adding the check therefore means a wire slot for the presenter to ship the
session document, a decision about what an absent or unattributable session
document resolves to (a task digest attests content, not authenticity — it is
load-bearing only because the credential's *issuer* signed it), a new host
verdict beside `WitnessBinding`, and a default-policy change to branch on it.
That is design work. #1068 stays open for it, alongside item 1 (implement the
witness role) and the `assert`-path gap.

What *is* in this PR is the issuing-side half, which is small and clearly
correct: `a_catalog_built_vwc_carries_the_required_task_context` now also
asserts that the VWC carries the session document's own task digest and that
`cites_task` resolves both halves back to the document it was built from. That
pins the two implementations together the same way the digest round-trip below
it already does.

### Where else `task_digest_multibase` belongs

Checked, and the answer is nowhere yet in this workspace:

- **No production issuing site exists.** `new_vwc*` appears only in the two test
  helpers above; the witness role (#1068 item 1) is unimplemented, so there is
  no VWC-issuing code path that could carry the field.
- **`vtc-service/src/credentials/task_context.rs`** answers a different question
  (which exchange a credential was *presented* in) and is blocked on the same
  missing document.
- **`vta_sdk::protocols::vetting`** carries a `task_context` on the vetting
  statement, and `vetting/session/0.1` does publish a `taskDigestMultibase` —
  it is the vector dtg-credentials 0.11 tests itself against. But that type is
  generated from the Trust Task registry, so the field lands in
  dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf first and reaches here through a `trust-tasks-rs` bump,
  never as a local edit.

### `vti-rooms-dtg` takes the workspace requirement

It carried a literal `dtg-credentials = "0.9.1"` while every other consumer took
`{ workspace = true }`. That is the drift `vti-rooms-wasm`'s manifest comment
argues against in so many words: a chain built by one version and verified by
another is refused as a *broken chain* rather than as a version skew. It now
takes the workspace requirement, so it cannot fall out of step again.

### Why `!`

`vti-rooms-dtg` publishes, and `open_credential` is `pub` and returns
`DTGCredential`. That makes `dtg-credentials`' version part of its public API,
so moving the requirement across a breaking release is a breaking change to the
crate itself — the re-export rule in CLAUDE.md, and the same shape as the
`ApproveScope` skew that rule was written for.

### Verification

`cargo tree -d` shows exactly one `dtg-credentials` in the graph (0.11.0). No
crate's own `version =` field was touched.

### Test results

- `cargo test --workspace --exclude vtc-service --exclude vtc-client --no-fail-fast` —
  **128 targets, 4814 passed, 0 failed.** The first run of this job failed once, in
  `vti-rooms-dtg` (the fixture above); green after the fix.
- `cargo test -p vtc-service -p vtc-client --no-fail-fast` — **67 targets, 1865 passed,
  0 failed.** `VTC_SKIP_ADMIN_UI_BUILD` was not set.
- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings` — clean.
- `cargo fmt --all -- --check` — clean.

Those runs were made before the rebase onto `a07f83ce`. After it, `cargo fmt --all --
--check` and the VTC job were re-run locally (67 targets, 1865 passed, 0 failed), and CI
ran the whole suite on the rebased head: Test (workspace), Test (VTC), Clippy, Format,
MSRV, cargo-deny and the rest all pass.

title: docs(spec): release framework version 0.6.1
body:
Patch release addressing the review of WD 0.6.0 from NAOMS. It contains errata, clarified prose and repaired examples only. The wire format and what a conforming Trust Task specification must declare are unchanged, so this is a PATCH under §5.1.1.

## Changes

- **Examples sign with `eddsa-jcs-2022`.** Example 1 and the error-response example carried `eddsa-rdfc-2022`, while the reference ecosystem signs with JCS. Both suites are conformant, but implementers copy examples. (NAOMS Q3)
- **The Abstract states the bilateral model.** It said "between two or more parties" while §3 defines every document as bilateral. (NAOMS drafting note)
- **Group as a party (non-normative note in §4.8).** A group holding authority jointly, e.g. under a threshold key, is a party when it has its own VID. Which members may act for it is authorization (Consumer Requirements item 10), not the envelope's job. (NAOMS Proposal 1)
- `Document Status` → Working Draft 0.6.1, and an Appendix B entry.

## Not in this PR

- **A mandatory-to-implement cryptosuite (NAOMS Q4)** is a Task Force decision.
- **The Type URI change (NAOMS Proposal 2)** is #20. That one is a MINOR (0.7.0) since it widens what a private specification may declare. If this PR merges first, #20's "Unreleased" changelog entry lands above 0.6.1.
- **Registry companions** (tracked in dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf): the `acl/change-role/0.1` example cryptosuite, and publishing the `trust-task/0.6.1` framework URI after merge.

Rendered locally with `npm run render`: no errors, and every in-page anchor resolves.

title: Let a private Type URI be any absolute URI
body:
## Why

§6.1 required every Type URI to use `https`. The reason given protects consumers that *dereference* the URI, but a consumer matches `type` by exact string and never has to dereference it. The rule tied every specification's name to DNS and a CA for no benefit to those consumers, and it shut out implementers with no DNS presence (raised by NAOMS against WD 0.6.0).

## What changes

- **Public registry: unchanged.** `https://trusttasks.org/spec/<slug>/<MAJOR.MINOR>`, and registry specs MUST use it.
- **Private specs: any absolute URI.** This includes https, a DID URL, a URN, or another scheme.
  - Path form (everything except URNs): `<prefix>/spec/<slug>/<MAJOR.MINOR>`
  - URN form: `urn:<NID>:<prefix>:spec:<slug-segments>:<MAJOR.MINOR>`, with the slug's `/` written as `:`
  - Slug and version extraction is defined for both forms.
- **`http` stays non-conformant** in every form.
- **A Type URI is a name.** This is now stated: consumers match it by exact string equality and need not dereference it. Content negotiation applies to `https` only. Other schemes rely on out-of-band distribution, with the schema's source authenticated per Schema-Validation DoS.
- Producer requirement 3 and spec requirement 7.5 no longer assume content negotiation.
- Fixes the private example that omitted the `/spec/` segment the slug rule depends on.
- Changelog entry under **Unreleased** in Appendix B.

## Compatibility

Additive: every document conforming to 0.6.0 still conforms. The SDK Type URI parsers need follow-ups in `dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf` before they can accept non-https private forms. For example, `trust-tasks-rs/src/type_uri.rs` rejects any scheme other than `https`.

Rendered locally with `npm run render`: no errors, and every in-page anchor resolves.

title: Guard the explore guide's pinned release in CI
body:
Refs #40

The explore guide has operators download `setup-explore.sh` from a tagged release and check it against a SHA-256 pinned on the page, because they then run it as root. Nothing checks that pin, so two failures are invisible:

- **drift** — the pin stops describing the script in the tree, and the guide tells operators to reject the current release;
- **missing** — the pinned release was never published, so both downloads 404 and the explore stream stops at its first command.

The second is the state of `main` today, and is what #40 reports.

`guard-release-pin.sh` covers both. It takes the version, the hash **and the download URL** from `sysop/explore/01-server-setup.md` itself rather than restating any of them, so it checks the URL operators are actually told to fetch — the same approach `guard-remote-exec.sh` takes of grepping the real pages.

**Why the triggers are split.** `RELEASING.md` deliberately pins the version and hash in a merged PR *before* the tag that publishes the release exists. A guard demanding the release on every pull request would block the very PR that makes the release possible. So:

| check | trigger | today |
| --- | --- | --- |
| pin matches `scripts/setup-explore.sh` | every PR, push, schedule | passes |
| pinned release is published and matches | push to `main` + daily cron | **fails until `v1.0.0` is tagged** |

**That second failure is intentional and is the point.** It is the bug in #40 becoming visible; it goes green when the tag is pushed, with no further change here. If you would rather land the tag first and this after, say so and I will hold it.

### Verified

`shellcheck scripts/*.sh .github/scripts/*.sh` — clean, exit 0, all three scripts (shellcheck 0.11.0).

Behaviour, exercised against a local HTTP server standing in for the release:

| case | result |
| --- | --- |
| pin matches the tree | passes |
| pinned release absent (real `v1.0.0`) | fails, names the tag and points at RELEASING.md |
| script edited, pin not re-pinned | fails, prints both hashes |
| `VER=` or `SHA256=` missing from the guide | fails |
| release published and matching | passes |
| published asset does not match the pin | fails, prints both hashes |
| release `SHA256SUMS` disagrees with its own asset | fails |

The guide is read with `tr -d '\r'` so a checkout made with `core.autocrlf=true` parses the same way the runner does. The script hash itself is deliberately taken from the file as it stands, matching what `release.yml` hashes.

title: Fix two links that 404 on GitHub, and run the documented markdown lint in CI
body:
Closes #41

Two independent one-line fixes to the same repo, kept in one PR because both are housekeeping. Happy to split.

**Links.** `developer/01-personal-vta.md` linked to `/sysop/explore/01-server-setup.md` twice. A leading `/` resolves against `github.com`, not the repository, so both rendered as `https://github.com/sysop/explore/01-server-setup.md` — 404. One of the two is in **Prerequisites**, so it is the first link the developer journey asks anyone to follow. Changed to `../sysop/explore/01-server-setup.md`, which is the form `developer/README.md` already uses. I checked every relative link in the repo; these were the only two broken ones.

**Lint.** `CLAUDE.md` documents `markdownlint-cli2 "**/*.md"` and `.markdownlint.json` is committed, but `lint.yml` ran only shellcheck and the remote-exec guard — nothing linted the markdown in a documentation-only repo. Added a `markdown` job, action pinned to a commit SHA the way `actions/checkout` already is (`markdownlint-cli2-action` v24.2.0 bundles `markdownlint-cli2` 0.23.2).

The tree is already clean under the committed config, so the job repairs nothing and starts green:

```
$ markdownlint-cli2 "**/*.md"
Linting: 14 files
Summary: 0 issues in 0 files
```

No instruction, command or behaviour changes — link targets and a CI job only.

Note: this touches `lint.yml`, as does the PR for the release-pin guard. Whichever lands second, I will rebase.

## 🤖 New release * `vta-sdk`: 0.49.0 -> 0.49.1 (✓ API compatible changes) * `vti-common`: 0.23.0 -> 0.23.1 (✓ API compatible changes) * `vta-cli-common`: 0.22.0 -> 0.22.1 (✓ API compatible changes) * `pnm-cli`: 0.21.0 -> 0.21.1 * `vta-service`: 0.39.0 -> 0.39.1 (✓ API compatible changes)
Changelog

## `vta-sdk`

## [0.49.1](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/compare/vta-sdk-v0.49.0...vta-sdk-v0.49.1) — 2026-09-22 ### Added - **cli**: Pnm reaches worlds and the claim-type registry ([#1663](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1663)) `persona/facet/{put,list,delete}` and `persona/claim-types/list` had no method on `VtaClient` at all, so `pnm` could not reach them even though both graphical clients do. The SDK gains the four, built from the generated specification types rather than hand-written bodies, and decoding their responses into the generated `Response` — a shape the specification does not describe is then an error at the call rather than a `None` three screens later. `pnm persona world {list,put,delete}` and `pnm persona claim-types` follow. Both id lists on a put replace: the specification is explicit that a member whose absence meant "keep" would make emptying a world impossible, so the CLI passes them through as given and says so. The colour is a ValueEnum whose mapping to the specification's tokens is written out rather than derived, pinned from both sides — `pnm-cli` does not depend on the generated types and `vta-cli-common` does not know the CLI's enum, so the pair of tests is what holds the wire value end to end.
## `vti-common`
## [0.23.1](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/compare/vti-common-v0.23.0...vti-common-v0.23.1) — 2026-09-22 ### Fixed - **auth**: Consume the challenge before minting, atomically ([#1664](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1664)) `handle_authenticate` read the challenge row, checked it was in `ChallengeSent`, then looked up the ACL and minted tokens, and only after all that deleted the row. Those are awaits, and the row stayed alive across them, so two interleaved presentations of the same signed envelope both passed the state check and both minted. Sequentially it was correct; under concurrency the single-use challenge was not single-use ([#1656](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1656)). Sessions coalesce per DID (last write wins, access token pinned by `token_id`), so an attacker who captured a correctly-addressed envelope and replayed it inside the freshness window while the holder signed in could win the race, hold the session as the holder, and supersede the holder's own access token.
## `vta-cli-common`

title: fix(vtc): answer the auth tasks with the error codes their specs declare
body:
Follows #1649's error-code census, which left the five auth codes.

## What was wrong

`routes/auth.rs` and `routes/recognise.rs` used **no declared error code at all**. Every refusal was a status plus prose, so a client distinguishing "your credential did not hold up" from "this community grants your role nothing here" had to match on English.

## What now carries a code

| Code | Refusal |
|---|---|
| `vtc/auth/admin-session:invalidToken` | the mirrored access token did not verify — signature, audience or expiry |
| `vtc/auth/recognise:credentialInvalid` | the VEC or VMC failed proof verification, fell outside its validity window, or was revoked |
| `vtc/auth/recognise:roleNotMapped` | policy allowed the issuer but mapped the foreign role to no local role |

The last two are worth separating: `roleNotMapped` is an operator's policy decision about roles, `credentialInvalid` is the credential itself. A caller acts differently on each.

**`credentialInvalid` is applied to exactly what the spec describes** — "failed proof verification, was expired, or was revoked via credentialStatus", i.e. `ProofInvalid`, `StatusListFailed`, `ValidityWindow`, plus the zero-window case at mint, which is "was expired" arriving a moment later. `IssuerKeyUnresolved` and `Malformed` stay **uncoded**: they are refusals about a document that could not be checked at all rather than one that was checked and failed, and filing them under this code would misdescribe them. A unit test pins that.

## One thing worth reviewing

Both handlers now return `TaskError` instead of `AppError`. That is not cosmetic: `From<TaskError> for AppError` deliberately **drops** the code (for surfaces that cannot carry one), so a handler returning `AppError` would have constructed each code and thrown it away. The first version of this change did exactly that and looked fine.

## The census

Baseline 11 → 8. The two remaining auth codes are **not** missing tests, and the baseline now records why rather than leaving the next person to re-derive it:

- **`rateLimited`** — declared by the challenge task, but the limiter in front of it is the chain-wide per-IP governor. `governor_error_response` receives a `GovernorError` with no request, so it cannot know which route was refused and cannot name a route-scoped code. Emitting this means giving the limiter route context first.
- **`issuerNotRecognised`** — comes from the trust registry answering "no". Every fixture in the tree wires `registry_client: None`, so the route stops at the registry pre-flight and the gate never runs. Witnessing it means building a registry stub.

I would rather leave those two visible in the baseline with a reason than manufacture a witness that asserts against a mock of our own refusal.

## Tests

- `the_admin_session_task_answers_with_the_invalid_token_code_its_spec_declares` — a junk token and a token minted for another audience, both through the route.
- `the_recognise_task_answers_with_the_codes_its_spec_declares` — the role-mapping and expired-credential refusals, rendered and read back as a client sees them.
- `caller_rejections_stay_403` extended: each mapped variant carries its code, and `Malformed` carries none.

`cargo test -p vtc-service`: 1843 passed, 0 failed. `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings`: clean. The census test passes with the new witnesses and the lowered baseline.

title: vtc/vetting: a by-DID vetter status lookup (revoked vs unlisted) — Keyring VTI-Q3
body:
From Keyring's VTI-Q3.

`vtc/vetting/vetters/list/0.1` skips a vetter with no published profile and a vetter with no live grant alike. So an applicant can't tell from the list whether its vetter was **revoked** or is merely **unlisted**. Today the only way to find out is the grant credential's own status list.

**Decision:** a by-DID lookup task (something like `vtc/vetting/vetters/show/0.1`) that returns one vetter's grant status: `live`, `revoked`, `expired` or `none`, plus the grant id where there is one.

It's a new task rather than a `status` member on the existing list response, because adding a member to a Trust Task response breaks stale Rust consumers (`deny_unknown_fields`). The spec goes first, in dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf, then the VTC route and a vtc-client method.

title: feat(vtc/vetting/vetters/show): a by-DID vetter status lookup
body:
Adds `vtc/vetting/vetters/show/0.1`. This is the spec half of OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure#1651, which came from Keyring's VTI-Q3.

## Why

`vtc/vetting/vetters/list` omits a vetter with no published profile and a vetter whose grant was revoked in exactly the same way: both are simply absent. So:

- an applicant mid-exchange with a vetter who has gone quiet cannot tell whether that vetter was removed or never chose to be listed;
- a vetter cannot check their own standing at all.

The only way to find out today is to read the grant credential's own status list, which requires already holding the credential.

## What it answers

By DID: `live`, `revoked`, `expired` or `none`, plus `grantId`, the timestamp that ended or will end it, and — for a live grant — `listed`, which is what separates "a vetter who chose not to be listed" from "not a vetter".

A **new task** rather than a `status` member on the listing response: adding a member to an existing response is breaking for consumers that reject unknown members, and the two answer different questions — the listing is discovery, this is a lookup about someone you can already name.

## Three judgement calls worth reviewing

1. **`revoked` outranks `expired`** where both hold. Withdrawal and lapse are different statements about the community's trust, and an applicant reads them differently.
2. **`none` does not distinguish a non-member from a member who is not a vetter.** The caller asked about vetting; membership is not theirs to learn here. Conformance also asks that the answer cost the same whatever the status, so timing does not leak what the payload withholds.
3. **The revocation reason is not carried**, including through `ext`, which the Security & Privacy section says explicitly. It is the community's internal record and frequently concerns a third party; the caller needs to know the grant does not hold.

The response is also deliberately *not* evidence: a grant can be revoked a second after the answer is sent, so the spec says a `live` answer must not be treated as durable proof of eligibility — that is what the vetter's credential in `vetting/request` is for.

## Checks

- `npm run validate`: 473 specs, no errors, and no warning against this spec.
- `npm run build`: passes; all three examples validate against the framework envelope.
- Bindings regenerated for **Rust, TypeScript and Go** — the Go drift check in `.github/workflows/go.yml` makes that third one required, though the contributing guide lists only two.
- `cargo test -p trust-tasks-rs`: passes.
- No version bumps and no changelog entries, per RELEASING.md — the Release PR assigns those.

title: feat(vta): advertise TSP on a minted DID when the mediator carries it
body:
Closes #1652 (Keyring VTI-Q11).

## The problem

A persona minted by a TSP-capable VTA advertised only `DIDCommMessaging`, so a Rev 3 client reading its document kept the applicant ↔ vetter leg on DIDComm.

The cause is narrower than it looks: `addTspService` defaulted to `false` at the mint, and **a persona is minted by a caller that sends no such field** — `vta-sdk` skips it on the wire when false. So the answer was always "no", however TSP-capable the VTA and its mediator were.

## The change

`addTspService` becomes three-state, and only the absent case is new:

| Wire | Before | Now |
|---|---|---|
| `true` | `#tsp` (subject to the existing gates) | unchanged |
| `false` | no `#tsp` | unchanged |
| absent | **no `#tsp`** | `#tsp` iff this VTA and its mediator carry TSP |

"Carries TSP" is the check VTA setup already makes for the VTA's own document: `services.tsp` is on, a mediator is configured, and that mediator's DID document advertises `TSPTransport`.

**An unresolvable mediator answers no** — deliberately stricter than setup, which warns and proceeds. There the operator named the mediator deliberately and sees the warning; here nobody asked for `#tsp` at all, so the quiet default must not publish a transport peers cannot reach the DID on.

Every internal caller now passes `Some(false)` explicitly, so no existing path changes behaviour. No SDK change is needed: it already omits the field when false, which is exactly the "absent" case.

## Tests

- `tsp_is_advertised_only_when_the_vta_and_its_mediator_both_carry_it` — drives the decision against **real, resolvable** `did:peer` mediators, one advertising `TSPTransport` and one not, plus the VTA-not-TSP, no-mediator and unresolvable cases. The positive and negative mediators differ only in that service, so the check is what decides.
- `an_explicit_request_wins_over_the_capability_default` — silence asks the mediator; `Some(false)` still means no however capable the stack is; `Some(true)` passes through to the existing downstream gates.

`cargo test -p vta-service -p vta-sdk`: 2705 passed, 0 failed. `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings`: clean.

## Related, not in scope

Keyring VTI-Q2: openvtc's vetting inbound path is DIDComm-only, so once a persona advertises `#tsp` it would need a TSP receive leg before a Rev 3 peer could use it. That is in the reference client, not here.

title: vta-service 0.39.0 on crates.io does not build: the semver baseline fails rustdoc
body:
Noticed while merging #1664, whose semver job failed for this reason and not for anything in that PR.

## What

The semver report aborts with:

```
error: aborting due to failure to build rustdoc for crate vta-service v0.39.0
PUBLISHED CRATE DOES NOT BUILD: vta-service -- the semver baseline is the published
crate as a consumer receives it, so a baseline that fails to build means consumers
cannot build it either.
```

The job's own message says how to reproduce it:

```sh
cargo new --lib x && cd x && echo '[workspace]' >> Cargo.toml
cargo add vta-service && cargo build
```

## Why it matters

This is not "the check could not run". The baseline is the crate exactly as a consumer receives it from crates.io, so if rustdoc cannot build it there, a consumer adding `vta-service` to a fresh project has the same problem. Every other crate in the sweep passed (`vti-common` 196/196, `vti-rooms`, `vti-rooms-dtg`, `vti-secrets` all "no semver update required"), so this is specific to `vta-service` as published, not a workspace-wide breakage.

It also means the semver report stays red for every PR until it is fixed, which is the failure mode where a permanently-red informational check stops being read. That is the second cost, and the reason to fix it rather than note it.

## Worth checking first

- Whether the published 0.39.0 is missing a file or a feature the manifest implies (a `include`/`exclude` slip, or a path dependency that resolved locally but not from the registry).
- Whether it builds but only *rustdoc* fails — the error names rustdoc specifically, and a doc-only failure (an intra-doc link to something behind a disabled feature, say) is a different fix from a compile failure.

Unowned; filed so the red report has a home rather than being re-diagnosed on the next PR.

title: fix(auth): consume the challenge before minting, atomically
body:
Closes #1656.

## The bug

`handle_authenticate_with_aal` consumed a single-use challenge as a read-then-write:

1. `get_session(session_id)`
2. refuse unless `state == ChallengeSent`
3. challenge compare, TTL, signer, freshness
4. `check_acl(...)` — **await**
5. `mint_session_tokens(...)` — **await**, signing work
6. `store_session(...)`, then `delete_session(challenge row)`

The check at (2) was the only guard, and the row that invalidates it survived until (6). The window is not sub-millisecond: it spans an ACL lookup and a mint. Two interleaved presentations of the same signed envelope both passed (2), and both minted.

Because sessions coalesce per DID (last write wins, access token pinned by `token_id`), the winner holds the live session **as the holder** and the loser's access token is immediately superseded. So an attacker who captured a correctly-addressed signed envelope and replayed it inside the 5-minute freshness window, racing a genuine sign-in, could take the holder's session and knock out the holder's own token.

Sequential replay was never the issue — it is refused with `SessionStateMismatch`, and affinidi/affinidi-webvh-service#208 added route tests for that at three services.

## The fix

`SessionStore::take_session` — read **and** remove, a claim rather than a look. The handler takes the challenge row before the ACL lookup and the mint, and refuses the caller who did not get it.

**This is not a new pattern.** The same trait already closes exactly this TOCTOU on the refresh path with `take_session_id_by_refresh`, documented as cross-replica safe (Redis `GETDEL`, DynamoDB `DeleteItem ReturnValues=ALL_OLD`, fjall mutex). The authenticate path simply never got the same treatment — an omission, not a design choice.

**Non-breaking, by choice.** The trait method has a default implementation that keeps today's `get_session` + `delete_session`, so every existing backend — including webvh's three services and the in-crate test backends — compiles unchanged and none silently changes behaviour. The default is documented as *not* atomic; `KeyspaceSessionStore` overrides it with the keyspace's atomic `take_raw`, so the VTC and VTA get the real claim immediately.

A challenge row is always uuid-keyed (`handle_challenge` mints a v4), so taking it can never remove the DID-keyed row of an established session.

## Tests

`two_presentations_of_one_challenge_mint_once` interleaves two presentations of the same envelope and asserts exactly one mints. **Revert the ordering and it fails with two successes** — two complete token bundles issued for one challenge. I checked that, so the test discriminates rather than passing either way.

`the_default_take_session_reads_and_removes` pins the non-atomic default's behaviour, since a backend that never overrides depends on it.

`cargo test --workspace`: 6746 passed, 0 failed. `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings`: clean.

## Follow-up, not in scope here

Any other single-use row consumed the same way deserves the same look. The refresh path is already correct; nothing else was audited as part of this.

title: handle_authenticate consumes the challenge non-atomically: a replayed sign-in can win a race
body:
Found while answering code-scanning alerts on affinidi/affinidi-webvh-service#208 (the recipient-binding fix, the webvh relay of #1638). The scanner hedged on "if session/challenge consumption is not atomic". It isn't.

## What

`vti_common::auth::handlers::handle_authenticate_with_aal` (`src/auth/handlers/authenticate.rs`) consumes a single-use challenge as a read-then-write, with no compare-and-swap and no lock:

1. `get_session(&input.session_id)`
2. refuse unless `session.state == SessionState::ChallengeSent`
3. constant-time challenge compare, challenge TTL, signer check, freshness
4. `check_acl(&session.did)` — an await
5. `mint_session_tokens(...)` — an await, signing work
6. `store_session(&auth_session)`, then `delete_session(&input.session_id)`

The `ChallengeSent` check at step 2 is the only guard, and the row that would invalidate it is not removed until step 6. The window is not sub-millisecond: it spans an ACL lookup and token minting.

`AuthBackend::SessionStore` offers only `store_session`, `get_session` and `delete_session` (`src/auth/backend.rs:172-178`) — there is no primitive with which a caller could make this atomic.

## Impact

Two sufficiently interleaved presentations of the same signed sign-in both pass step 2 and both mint. Since sessions coalesce per DID (last write wins, access token pinned by `token_id`), the loser's access token is immediately superseded. So an attacker who captured a correctly-addressed signed envelope, and replays it inside the 5-minute freshness window while the holder signs in, can win the race and hold the live session **as the holder**, invalidating the holder's own access token.

Preconditions are narrow: the attacker needs the holder's signed envelope, within the freshness window, and has to interleave with a real sign-in. It is a race, not a straightforward replay — the sequential replay path is correctly refused (`SessionStateMismatch`), and webvh #208 now has tests for that at all three of its routes.

## Suggested fix

Consume the challenge before the expensive work, not after: add a compare-and-delete (or compare-and-swap on `state`) to `SessionStore`, take the row at step 2, and mint only if this caller is the one that took it. A backend without an atomic primitive can serialise per `session_id`.

The same shape applies to any other single-use row consumed this way — the refresh path is worth checking alongside it.

## Not affected

- Sequential replay: refused, and the state check logs it as a replay.
- webvh #208: unrelated to that change; the recipient binding is orthogonal and lands independently.

title: fix(auth): consume the challenge before minting, atomically (#1664)
body:
fix(auth): consume the challenge before minting, atomically (#1664)

`handle_authenticate` read the challenge row, checked it was in
`ChallengeSent`, then looked up the ACL and minted tokens, and only after
all that deleted the row. Those are awaits, and the row stayed alive across
them, so two interleaved presentations of the same signed envelope both
passed the state check and both minted. Sequentially it was correct; under
concurrency the single-use challenge was not single-use (#1656).

Sessions coalesce per DID (last write wins, access token pinned by
`token_id`), so an attacker who captured a correctly-addressed envelope and
replayed it inside the freshness window while the holder signed in could win
the race, hold the session as the holder, and supersede the holder's own
access token.

`SessionStore::take_session` is the claim: exactly one concurrent caller
observes `Some`. The handler now takes the row before the ACL lookup and the
mint, and refuses the loser as it refuses a replay. This is the treatment
`take_session_id_by_refresh` already gives the refresh path — the
authenticate path was an omission, not a different design.

The default implementation keeps today's `get` + `delete`, so every backend
compiles unchanged and none silently changes behaviour; it is documented as
not atomic, and `KeyspaceSessionStore` overrides it with the keyspace's
atomic `take_raw` (Redis GETDEL / DynamoDB DeleteItem ALL_OLD / fjall mutex).

title: spec(messaging/account): opt-in lifetime counters on account/get and account/list
body:
## What

`Account` gains an optional **`stats`** object, so an operator can read an account's lifetime totals from the mediator rather than counting locally from a live traffic feed:

- `messagesReceived` / `messagesSent`, and `bytesReceived` / `bytesSent`
- `receivedByProtocol` / `sentByProtocol` — the same counts split by wire protocol (`didcomm`, `didcommV1`, `tsp`, `other`), which is what makes a protocol mix answerable per account rather than per connection

Every member is optional: a mediator reports what it keeps, and a counter absent from a response was **not kept**, rather than zero. The counters survive restarts, reading them does not reset them, and removing an account discards them.

## Why opt-in

`account/get` and `account/list` each gain an optional request member, `includeStats`, exactly like `includeActivity`. A mediator returns `stats` only when it is `true`, and **MUST NOT** otherwise.

The generated clients reject unknown members, so a mediator that always sent `stats` would break every requester built against the older schema. In the other direction, a requester that sends `includeStats` to an older mediator gets a schema rejection, so the prose says to set it only where the mediator is known to support it.

The change is additive inside version 0.1 of `messaging/account/{get,list}`: every existing document stays valid.

## Also

- Security & Privacy notes for both tasks: the counters disclose volume rather than content, and get the same authorization as the rest of the account view.
- All four client libraries regenerated. `npm run build`, `npm run check-bindings` and `cargo test -p trust-tasks-rs` pass.

title: feat(cli): pnm reaches worlds and the claim-type registry
body:
`persona/facet/{put,list,delete}` and `persona/claim-types/list` had **no method on `VtaClient`** — not merely no CLI verb — so `pnm` could not reach worlds or the claim-type registry at all, while both graphical clients do.

**SDK.** Four new methods on the persona slice, built from `trust_tasks_rs::specs` rather than hand-written bodies, and decoding into the generated `Response`. The older methods on that slice return `Value` because they predate the generated modules; these do not, so a response the specification does not describe is an error at the call rather than a `None` three screens later.

**CLI.** `pnm persona world {list,put,delete}` and `pnm persona claim-types`.

- **Both id lists on a put replace.** Omitting `--face` empties the world rather than leaving it alone — the specification is explicit that a member whose absence meant "keep" would make emptying one impossible. The help says so and points at `world list`.
- **Delete leaves every member where it was.** There is no cascading form; the response's `releasedFaces` is how many faces now belong to no world.
- **The colour's mapping to the specification's tokens is written out, not derived.** Pinned from both sides, because `pnm-cli` does not depend on the generated types and `vta-cli-common` does not know the CLI's enum: `pnm-cli` checks the eight tokens its enum offers, `vta-cli-common` checks those tokens all parse as a `FacetColour`.
- A bad ULID names itself, rather than reporting a pattern failure against whichever of six repeated flags was wrong.

`docs/02-vta/claim-type-registry.md` gains a line pointing at `pnm persona claim-types` — the table to read before wondering why a value came back masked.

CI set run locally: `cargo fmt --all -- --check`, `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings`, workspace tests (4817), `-p vtc-service -p vtc-client` (1831).

title: feat(console): contacts, formats, and faces made inside a context
body:
Three parts of the persona surface the console could not reach. Each already had an SDK call in `@openvtc/pnm-core/persona` with nothing importing it.

### People — `persona/contact/{put,get,list,delete}`
What others have told the holder about themselves, on the context card in the identity map. Filed against the persona this context knows, because "who was I when they told me this" is part of the record.

A card is a revision, not an overwrite, so the pane shows the revision number, offers what they said before, and surfaces `hasUnreviewedChange`. What the holder types is sent with no `provenance`: it is their note of what someone said, and claiming one on the peer's behalf would turn a note into an assertion about them.

### Formats — `persona/renderers/list`
A panel in the Released view, beside the disclosure history. The two answer halves of one question — what left, and what shape it left in. "Drops nothing" and "this agent does not offer it" are kept apart, per `dropsOf`'s own warning: rendering the second as the first tells a holder a format is safe when the disclosure is about to be refused.

### Faces made here — `persona/local/profile/{put,delete}`, `persona/local/binding/set`
The existing promote picker gains make, wear and delete. Delete sends `unbind`, since the question the holder answers says the face comes off as it goes; without it the agent refuses while it is worn and delete would work only sometimes. A made face is inline-only and self-asserted — that is the boundary, not a shortcut: a context-local face has nowhere in its wire type to name a pool attribute.

### Not included, deliberately
`persona/disclosure/{preview,present}` looked missing but is not: `background.ts` drives both from a page request through the consent window, by URI rather than through the SDK helpers. A console flow would be a second way to do the same thing.

Ran locally: `npm run lint`, `npm run build`, `npm test`, and every dist guard in `ci.yml` — MV3 single bundle, the admin, seeds and holder-scoped-persona confinement checks, console-carries-persona, and the console single-bundle check.

title: feat(tui): contacts, formats, purge, and faces made inside a community
body:
Everything in `persona/*` the identity pane could not reach, plus §5.8 of the persona design note.

| New | Task | Where |
|---|---|---|
| People | `persona/contact/{put,get,list,delete}` | `p` on a community |
| Formats | `persona/renderers/list` | `f` on Disclosures |
| Who it knows you as | `persona/binding/list` | `k` on a community |
| Forget earlier versions | `persona/attribute/purge-version` | `p` on an attribute |
| Make / wear / delete a face made here | `persona/local/profile/{put,delete}`, `persona/local/binding/set` | in the faces-made-here view |

**People.** Filed against the persona this community knows — "who was I when they told me this" is part of the record, so there is no picker. A card is a revision rather than an overwrite, so the detail shows what they said before and the list marks a change the holder has not looked at. What the holder types is sent with no provenance: it is their note of what someone said.

**Who it knows you as** warns when a community holds more than one of the holder's personas. Anyone reading both rows can see they are the same person, and no other row in the pane says so.

**Forget earlier versions** asks first and cannot be undone. The listing does not say which faces pin an *old* version, so the question names the faces at risk rather than claiming a number it cannot know, and the purge reports how many pins it actually broke.

**Worlds are offered rather than asked for** (§5.8): at four faces with none, the Faces tab says what they are for. The same threshold the browser console uses — below it a world arranges one thing, and an "add a world" step asks the holder to pre-think a taxonomy before they have the members.

**Esc withdraws one layer at a time.** A view holding a form, an armed question or an open record closes that first; dropping the whole view would throw away a half-typed card to answer "not that one".

`openvtc-core` gains `persona::contacts`, `pool::purge_versions`, `binding::{list,set_local}`, `disclosure::renderers` and `lifecycle::{local_face_put,local_face_delete}`.

CI set run locally: fmt, both clippy runs, doc, tests with `--include-ignored` (1510), `--no-default-features` (1491), `-p openvtc --features dev-overrides` (680), bench build.

title: trust-tasks-rs-v0.21.19
body:
### Added

- **specs**: Add the ExtCritical framework def, and open vetting requirements to ext ([#600](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/pull/600))

A community publishing an admission mode the join manifest does not
  enumerate has had two options: put the parameters in an undeclared
  member of `vetting` and watch them vanish, or wait for a version of the
  manifest that names them. This adds the third.

  framework 0.4 (specs/_framework/0.4/framework.schema.json)
    Additive over 0.3: `Ext` and `DigestMultibase` carried forward
    unchanged, `ExtCritical` new — the array naming the `ext` namespaces
    a consumer must understand or refuse, per the framework change in
    trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-spec#23. Neither rule it carries is
    checkable by JSON Schema: that an entry names a namespace present in
    the sibling `ext` is checkable only against that sibling, and whether
    a namespace is load-bearing is not a schema question. The $def says
    so, and both are consumer-side checks.

  vtc/join-requests/manifest 0.2 (draft, edited in place per SPEC §5.2)
    `vetting` gains `ext` and `extCritical`, and this draft's framework
    $refs re-pin from 0.2 to 0.4, errata-style.

    `vetting` was already `additionalProperties: true`, so an undeclared
    member always validated. Validating is not arriving: a generated type
    names the members the schema declares and drops the rest, so the
    member was parsed and discarded, and discarded again on the
    re-serialization `requirementsDigest` is computed over — a reader
    recomputing the digest from what it parsed got a value that did not
    match what it was sent. A declared member survives both.

    A new response example shows a criterion carrying hidden-vetting
    parameters under a namespace it controls, marked critical because an
    applicant that ignored it would gather named statements and present
    them to a criterion whose purpose is that it never receives them. Its
    `requirementsDigest` is the real value for the criterion as printed.

  Generated bindings regenerated: 472 specs across TypeScript, Rust, Go
  and Dart all agree. `npm run validate` passes 472 specs; the manifest's
  validate-gated fixtures run 5 tests; `cargo test --workspace` is 927.



### Documentation

- **specs**: Sign examples with eddsa-jcs-2022 ([#599](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/pull/599))

* docs(specs): sign examples with eddsa-jcs-2022

  30 draft specifications' examples carried "cryptosuite":
  "eddsa-rdfc-2022", while the reference ecosystem signs with
  eddsa-jcs-2022. Both suites are conformant, but implementers copy
  examples, and the two canonicalize differently. Raised by NAOMS against
  acl/change-role/0.1 (framework spec PR #21 makes the same fix to the
  framework's own examples).

  Editorial, made in place per CONTRIBUTING-SPECS: examples only, no
  schema or wire change, no version folder. The 20 retired specifications
  that carry the same example are frozen (SPEC §6.4) and left as they are.

title: feat(specs): add the ExtCritical framework def, and open vetting requirements to ext
body:
Companion to **trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-spec#23**, which adds the criticality marking to the framework text. This is the schema half plus the first specification to use it.

## The problem it fixes

A community publishing an admission mode the join manifest does not enumerate — the parameters of a zero-knowledge vetting scheme, in the case that prompted this — has had two options: put them in an undeclared member of `vetting` and watch them disappear, or wait for a manifest version that names them.

`vetting` is `additionalProperties: true`, so an undeclared member has always **validated**. That is not the same as **arriving**. A generated type carries the members its schema declares and drops the rest, so the member is discarded on the way in — and discarded again on the re-serialization `requirementsDigest` is computed over, so a reader that recomputes the digest from what it parsed gets a value that does not match the one it was sent. An open object and an open type are different things, and only the declared member is both.

## What is here

**`specs/_framework/0.4/framework.schema.json`** — additive over 0.3 on the pattern 0.3's own description sets out: `Ext` and `DigestMultibase` carried forward unchanged, `ExtCritical` new.

Neither rule `ExtCritical` carries is checkable by JSON Schema, and the $def says so rather than implying otherwise: that an entry names a namespace present in the sibling `ext` is checkable only against that sibling, and whether a namespace is load-bearing is not a schema question at all. Both are consumer-side checks.

**`vtc/join-requests/manifest/0.2`** — a draft, so edited in place per SPEC §5.2. `vetting` gains `ext` and `extCritical`; this draft's framework $refs re-pin from 0.2 to 0.4, errata-style, with no change to any payload's effective wire shape.

A new response example shows a criterion carrying its parameters under a namespace it controls and marking that namespace critical — an applicant that ignored it would gather named statements and present them to a criterion whose whole purpose is that it never receives them, so it stops with `unsupportedExtension` instead of applying the wrong way. Its `requirementsDigest` is the real value for the criterion as printed; I verified the routine by recomputing the existing example's published digest first.

## Ordering

The prose links in `spec.md` point only at §4.5.1, which exists today. Nothing here depends on #23 having merged, and no link into `SPEC.md` breaks while it has not — `SPEC.md` is generated from canonical `main`, so the anchor for the new sub-section appears when #23 lands and a follow-up can point at it precisely.

## Checks

- `npm run validate` — 472 specs, 1451 framework links against 154 anchors
- `npm run check-bindings` — 472 specifications across TypeScript, Rust, Go and Dart all agree; 903 error codes match
- `cargo test --workspace` — 927 tests
- `cargo test -p trust-tasks-rs --features "validate,vtc" …manifest::v0_2` — 5 tests, including the new example
- `npm run build` — clean

No version bump and no changelog entry: release-plz owns both.

title: feat(spec): let a producer mark an ext namespace critical
body:
## What

Adds `extCritical` — a sibling array naming `ext` namespaces a consumer must understand or refuse — plus the `unsupportedExtension` error code it rejects with.

## Why

`ext` (§4.5.1) is what lets a specification grow without a version increment, and rule 5 — *a consumer MUST ignore namespaces it does not recognize* — is what makes it safe. It also means a producer cannot distinguish an ignored namespace from an understood one.

That is fine while `ext` carries hints and annotations. It stops being fine as soon as a namespace changes what the document means: a consumer that silently drops it reaches a verdict the producer never asked for, and reaches it invisibly. Today a specification has only two options — put the data in `ext` and accept the silent downgrade, or promote it to a first-class member and bump the version. The second is what the extension point exists to avoid.

The concrete case: a community publishing zero-knowledge vetting parameters in its join manifest. A client that ignores them falls back to the named path and submits under a criterion the community may not accept that way. Nobody involved learns that a downgrade happened.

## The shape

Prior art is uniform — JOSE `crit`, X.509 critical extensions, TLS — so this follows it:

1. `extCritical` is an array of one or more unique namespace strings, allowed only where the specification allows `ext`, and only alongside a sibling `ext`.
2. Every entry must name a namespace actually present in that `ext`; an entry that does not is `malformedRequest`.
3. A consumer that does not recognize a critical namespace must reject with `unsupportedExtension` rather than ignore it. One that does recognize it proceeds exactly as before — criticality obliges a consumer to understand or refuse, never to act.
4. A producer must not mark a namespace whose absence leaves the document correct.
5. A producer should establish support first, through discovery or governance or out of band.

`extCritical` is covered by `proof` exactly as `ext` is, so on a signed document the marking cannot be stripped in transit; on an unsigned one it can, and the text says to sign if that matters.

## Trade-off, stated plainly

Criticality **reports** a downgrade; it does not prevent one. A producer that marks without establishing support has chosen a failed exchange over a silent one — the right trade only where the silent outcome is worse. That is why rules 5 and 6 sit on the producer, and why the error code is distinct: an operator seeing `unsupportedExtension` learns the counterparty understood the task and refused over one namespace, which `malformedRequest` would have hidden.

## Compatibility

Additive. Opting in is per specification and per object level, so no existing document changes meaning, and no consumer acquires work unless a producer marks something. A specification that allows `ext` and not `extCritical` rejects the member under its existing `additionalProperties: false`, and every namespace there stays ignorable.

No version header change: releases are their own commits here (#18), as with #17.

## Downstream

The framework schema `ExtCritical` $def and the first specification to opt in are a companion PR in `dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf`, where `SPEC.md` is generated from this repository.

title: feat(spec): let a producer mark an ext namespace critical (#23)
body:
feat(spec): let a producer mark an ext namespace critical (#23)

`ext` lets a specification grow without a version increment, and rule 5
makes a namespace safe to ignore. That is what makes it useful, and it
is also why a producer cannot tell an ignored namespace from an
understood one. A consumer that drops a namespace the document's
meaning depends on reaches a verdict the producer never asked for, and
reaches it invisibly.

This adds the marking that forecloses that, on the model of JOSE's
`crit`, X.509 critical extensions and TLS: a sibling `extCritical`
array naming namespaces that a consumer must understand or refuse.

- A new sub-section, Marking a Namespace Critical, with six rules: the
  member's shape, that every entry names a namespace present in the
  sibling `ext`, what critical means, the consumer's obligation,
  the producer's obligation not to mark what is merely useful, and the
  SHOULD to establish support before marking.
- A new standard error code, `unsupportedExtension`, distinct from
  `unsupportedType` and `unsupportedVersion`: the consumer understood
  the type and its version and refused over the namespace.
- Rule 5 of the ext section and the ext paragraph of Consumer
  Requirements each carry the exception.

Criticality reports a downgrade rather than preventing one, so the
producer rules are where the weight is: marking a namespace that is
merely useful turns every consumer that has not implemented it into a
failure where it would otherwise have interoperated. The text says so,
and says to establish support first.

Opting in stays per specification and per object level, so no existing
document changes meaning and no consumer has new work unless a producer
marks something.

title: test(vtc): hold the jsonschema resolvers off on the claimSchema path too
body:
#1660 turned off `resolve-http` and `resolve-file` and held the manifest
honest with a test on `/v1/schemas` and one on `validate_instance`. #1657
then added a third caller-supplied schema to the same compiler:
`check_schema`, run when an endorsement type is registered. It makes the same
`validator_for` call, so it carries the same exposure — restoring the features
would have been caught on two paths out of three.

The `file:` case is the decisive one: the referenced file really exists and
really is a valid schema, so the registration would succeed if the resolver
were on. The http case pins that the refusal happens at compile rather than
as an attempted fetch, and an internal `$ref` still registers, because this
removes remote resolution and not `$ref` itself.

title: fix(vtc): stop a caller's JSON Schema from fetching a URL or reading a file
body:
Closes the dependency half of #1657, handed over from that PR's author.

## The problem

The workspace pinned `jsonschema = "0.56"` and took its default features, which are `resolve-http`, `resolve-file`, `tls-aws-lc-rs`, `idna`. Every schema the VTC compiles comes from a caller:

- `POST /v1/schemas` — an admin's `credentialSchema` (on `main` today)
- `POST /v1/endorsement-types` — an admin's `claimSchema` (compiled at registration as of #1657)
- issuance — both again, via `validate_instance`

With those resolvers on, an external `$ref` makes the service fetch a URL or read a local file while compiling the schema.

## It reproduces

Not a theoretical gap — I checked both directions before and after the change:

| `jsonschema` features | `POST /v1/schemas` with `{"$ref": "file:///<a real file>"}` |
|---|---|
| default (before) | **201 Created** — the file was read and the schema stored |
| `default-features = false` (after) | **400** — refused at compile |

## The change

One manifest line: `default-features = false, features = ["idna"]`.

- `idna` is kept — it is the `hostname`/`idn-hostname` format check, pure computation, no I/O.
- `tls-aws-lc-rs` goes with `resolve-http`; it exists only to fetch over HTTPS.
- `Cargo.lock` drops `reqwest` and `rustls` from the jsonschema tree.

Nothing in the repo uses an external `$ref` (I grepped for `"$ref": "http(s)://"`), and a schema that needs one belongs inlined. Only `vtc-service` depends on jsonschema, so nothing else in the workspace is affected.

## Tests

One at each compile site, and **each fails if the features come back** — I verified that by re-enabling them, otherwise the tests would prove nothing:

- `vtc-service/src/schemas/validate.rs` — `an_external_ref_is_refused_rather_than_fetched`. The `file:` case is decisive: the target exists and is a valid schema, so it would compile if the resolver were on. Also asserts an ordinary internal `$ref` still resolves — this removes remote resolution, not `$ref`.
- `vtc-service/tests/endorsements.rs` — `register_schema_refuses_an_external_ref`, the same thing through the admin route.

`cargo test --workspace`: 6713 passed, 0 failed. `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings`: clean.

## Note for #1657

If this lands first, #1657 wants a rebase, and the same test is worth adding on the `claimSchema` registration path that PR introduces — that path compiles a caller's schema too, so it has the same exposure. No file overlap: this touches `Cargo.toml`, `Cargo.lock`, `schemas/validate.rs` and `tests/endorsements.rs`; #1657 touches the endorsement-type routes.

title: security(vtc)!: enforce the proof and freshness a Trust Task declares (VTI-OPS-020/021/024)
body:
The VTC's Trust Task document dispatcher verified a `proof` whenever one was
present and otherwise took attribution from the transport — including for the
nine dispatched tasks whose own definitions declare `proof` **REQUIRED**. It
applied no acceptance window to `issuedAt`, and the replay record it claimed
for every document was bounded by nothing but the guard's capacity.

That is the second of the two divergences Appendix F.2 records against this
service (trustoverip/dtgwg-vti-spec#35). It is the one the first depends on:
moving the 49 bearer-served tasks into the dispatcher closes nothing while the
dispatcher does not enforce.

`docs/05-design-notes/vtc-trust-task-proof-enforcement.md` has the argument,
the re-derived task census and the migration path.

## What is now enforced, on every transport

In `dispatch_trust_task_core`, before any handler runs, reached identically
from REST, DIDComm and TSP — which is VTI-OPS-021's whole point:

- **VTI-OPS-024** — an acceptance window over `issuedAt`: `max_age` 10 minutes,
  `skew` 60 seconds (SPEC §4.2's own "typically ≤ 60s"), `issuedAt` required.
  A future-dated `issuedAt` and an `expiresAt` at or before it are
  `malformedRequest`, not `expired` (SPEC §7.2 item 13 — neither was ever
  acceptable, so telling the producer to wait would be wrong).
- **VTI-OPS-020 / §7.2 items 5b, 7a, 8, §7.3 17** — the flag-driven rules the
  *specification* declares, via `schema_index::spec_policy_for(..).enforce(..)`:
  `recipient` REQUIRED, `proof` REQUIRED, audience binding, `issuedAt`
  REQUIRED. Read off the generated bindings by URI; there is no list of task
  URIs in this repository to drift from the registry.
- **VTI-OPS-020, the issuer binding** — a present proof must verify under a key
  the document's own `issuer` controls (SPEC §4.7). Previously a valid
  signature by *any* DID satisfied the requirement, establishing only that
  somebody signed something — which is not what `verified_signer` is read as by
  the `rooms/*` arms.
- **VTI-OPS-025…027** — the replay record is unchanged in mechanism but now
  *bounded*. `retain_until` caps a producer-chosen `expiresAt` at
  `issuedAt + max_age + skew`, so a document stamped `expiresAt = now + 10
  years` can no longer pin an id for ten years.

## What is not enforced, and why

**One client does not sign.** `openvtc-core` builds
`join-requests/{submit,status}`, `members/{self-remove,vmc}` and
`members/personhood/assert` with a deliberate "no `proof` is attached",
relying on the authcrypt sender or the TSP sender VID. `pnm-browser-plugin`,
`vtc-client` and `vta-sdk` sign on every channel.

So the one refusal that is gated is *a missing proof where the specification
declares one REQUIRED*: `[trust_tasks] require_declared_proof`, default
`false`. The allowance is narrow and loud —

- it relaxes a **missing** proof only, never an invalid one, never a missing
  `recipient` or `issuedAt`, never the audience-binding rule;
- it applies only where the transport authenticated the sender, so a REST
  document with no proof is refused whatever the setting;
- every waiver logs at `warn!` naming `VTI-OPS-021` and the task URI, so the
  debt is counted rather than assumed away.

A deployment serving only the three signing clients can set it to `true`
today and should.

**Its removal condition is exact**: when `openvtc-core` signs those five
documents, the default flips and the field goes with it. That is a one-line
change here and roughly five call sites there. No upstream specification change
is needed — `openvtc-core` already signs Trust Task documents on its vetting
path with the same `eddsa-jcs-2022` primitive.

**The transport cross-check (§7.2 item 6)** stays in the handlers
(`resolve_holder`), not the spine: a spine-level comparison of in-band `issuer`
against transport-derived sender would refuse the relayer ≠ holder shape this
workspace supports deliberately.

## What the next phase must do

1. `openvtc-core` signs. Flip the default, delete `require_declared_proof`.
   Divergence 2 closes.
2. Bind the 49 bearer-served proof-REQUIRED tasks in `DISPATCHED_URIS` /
   `dispatch_typed`, taking authorization from the verified signer's ACL entry.
   `auth/authenticate/0.1` and `vtc/relationships/publish/0.2` already do this
   and are the model.
3. Keep each bearer route as a documented transitional path with a stated
   removal point; the admin SPA, `cnm` and `vtc-client` need the signed path
   first.
4. Remove them, and close the Appendix F.2 entries.

One thing to carry into step 2: **VTI-OPS-027** requires the accepted-identifier
record to be shared across every binding. `REPLAY_GUARD` is process-local and
covers only the dispatcher, so a task served on both a bearer route and the
dispatcher would have a record on one binding and none on the other.

## Re-derived census, and its drift

Re-derived from `routes/mod.rs` (the single mount site) against
`spec_policy_for`, rather than taken from the register: **95** distinct task
URIs on REST routes, **51** declaring `proof` REQUIRED, of which two already
verify one — so **49** are served on a bearer token, not the 48 recorded. The
difference is exactly `vtc/invitations/deliver/0.1`, bound by #1648 after the
entry was written. `vtc/relationships/persona/0.1` has no published spec policy
in this build. No other drift.

## Why `!`

Three shapes that were accepted are now refused on the wire, on every
transport: a document with no `issuedAt` (or one outside a ten-minute window),
a document missing an in-band `recipient` its specification declares REQUIRED,
and a proof that verifies under a key the `issuer` does not control. Every
known producer already sends what is now required.

Refs #1641

- **VTI-OPS-020 / §7.2 items 5b, 7a, 8, §7.3 17** — the flag-driven rules the

  `recipient` REQUIRED, `proof` REQUIRED, audience binding, `issuedAt`
  REQUIRED. Read off the generated bindings by URI; there is no list of task
  URIs in this repository to drift from the registry.
- **VTI-OPS-020, the issuer binding** — a present proof must verify under a key
  the document's own `issuer` controls (SPEC §4.7). Previously a valid
  signature by *any* DID satisfied the requirement, establishing only that
  somebody signed something — which is not what `verified_signer` is read as by
  the `rooms/*` arms.
- **VTI-OPS-025…027** — the replay record is unchanged in mechanism but now
  *bounded*. `retain_until` caps a producer-chosen `expiresAt` at
  `issuedAt + max_age + skew`, so a document stamped `expiresAt = now + 10
  years` can no longer pin an id for ten years.

## What is not enforced, and why

**One client does not sign.** `openvtc-core` builds
`join-requests/{submit,status}`, `members/{self-remove,vmc}` and
`members/personhood/assert` with a deliberate "no `proof` is attached",
relying on the authcrypt sender or the TSP sender VID. `pnm-browser-plugin`,
`vtc-client` and `vta-sdk` sign on every channel.

So the one refusal that is gated is *a missing proof where the specification
declares one REQUIRED*: `[trust_tasks] require_declared_proof`, default
`false`. The allowance is narrow and loud —

- it relaxes a **missing** proof only, never an invalid one, never a missing
  `recipient` or `issuedAt`, never the audience-binding rule;
- it applies only where the transport authenticated the sender, so a REST
  document with no proof is refused whatever the setting;
- every waiver logs at `warn!` naming `VTI-OPS-021` and the task URI, so the
  debt is counted rather than assumed away.

A deployment serving only the three signing clients can set it to `true`
today and should.

**Its removal condition is exact**: when `openvtc-core` signs those five
documents, the default flips and the field goes with it. That is a one-line
change here and roughly five call sites there. No upstream specification change
is needed — `openvtc-core` already signs Trust Task documents on its vetting
path with the same `eddsa-jcs-2022` primitive.

**The transport cross-check (§7.2 item 6)** stays in the handlers
(`resolve_holder`), not the spine: a spine-level comparison of in-band `issuer`
against transport-derived sender would refuse the relayer ≠ holder shape this
workspace supports deliberately.

## What the next phase must do

1. `openvtc-core` signs. Flip the default, delete `require_declared_proof`.
   Divergence 2 closes.
2. Bind the 49 bearer-served proof-REQUIRED tasks in `DISPATCHED_URIS` /
   `dispatch_typed`, taking authorization from the verified signer's ACL entry.
   `auth/authenticate/0.1` and `vtc/relationships/publish/0.2` already do this
   and are the model.
3. Keep each bearer route as a documented transitional path with a stated
   removal point; the admin SPA, `cnm` and `vtc-client` need the signed path
   first.
4. Remove them, and close the Appendix F.2 entries.

One thing to carry into step 2: **VTI-OPS-027** requires the accepted-identifier
record to be shared across every binding. `REPLAY_GUARD` is process-local and
covers only the dispatcher, so a task served on both a bearer route and the
dispatcher would have a record on one binding and none on the other.

## Re-derived census, and its drift

Re-derived from `routes/mod.rs` (the single mount site) against
`spec_policy_for`, rather than taken from the register: **95** distinct task
URIs on REST routes, **51** declaring `proof` REQUIRED, of which two already
verify one — so **49** are served on a bearer token, not the 48 recorded. The
difference is exactly `vtc/invitations/deliver/0.1`, bound by #1648 after the
entry was written. `vtc/relationships/persona/0.1` has no published spec policy
in this build. No other drift.

## Why `!`

Three shapes that were accepted are now refused on the wire, on every
transport: a document with no `issuedAt` (or one outside a ten-minute window),
a document missing an in-band `recipient` its specification declares REQUIRED,
and a proof that verifies under a key the `issuer` does not control. Every
known producer already sends what is now required.

Refs #1641

title: Name a baseline cryptosuite every consumer can verify
body:
The framework left the proof cryptosuite open and named no floor. Two conforming implementations were therefore not guaranteed to verify each other's documents, which undercuts the two-interoperable-implementations bar for candidate (§5.3). NAOMS raised this as Q4 in their review of WD 0.6.0.

## The rules (new §4.7 "Cryptosuites")

- **Baseline:** every conforming consumer **MUST** verify `eddsa-jcs-2022`, which is Ed25519 over JCS. This is a floor on *verification*, not a constraint on signing. JCS is used because a Trust Task document is JSON whether or not it carries `@context`, so verifying one must not require a JSON-LD processor.
- **Choosing a suite:** the producer picks the suite from its key, and the consumer picks the verifier from `cryptosuite` plus the key type of `verificationMethod`. There is no negotiation member.
  - If the producer doesn't know what the consumer verifies, it SHOULD sign with the baseline.
  - It MAY use another suite where the spec, the trust framework, or the recipient's published keys indicate the consumer verifies it. For example, a party that publishes an ML-DSA key verifies ML-DSA.
- **P-256:** consumers **SHOULD** also verify `ecdsa-jcs-2019` with P-256, because secure enclaves, WebAuthn authenticators and many HSMs sign only with P-256.
- **Unsupported suite:** the consumer rejects the document with `proofInvalid`. It is never treated as unsigned.
- **Specs may require a suite:** added to Specification Requirements item 8, e.g. a quantum-resistant suite for long-lived evidence.
- **Quantum-resistant suites (draft):** `mldsa44-jcs-2024` (ML-DSA-44, multicodec `0x1210`) and `slhdsa128-jcs-2024` (SLH-DSA-SHA2-128s, `0x1220`), both using base64url multibase, are pinned to the W3C [Quantum-Resistant Cryptosuites v1.0](https://w3c.github.io/vc-di-quantum-resistant/) experimental draft.
  - They are agreed suites, not baseline.
  - If the draft changes, the change is adopted as a new entry and never reinterprets a pinned one.
  - We expect to move one into the baseline once there is a W3C Recommendation.

## Versioning

This adds a consumer obligation, so it is a **MINOR** change: it belongs in 0.7.0 with #20, not in the 0.6.1 patch (#21). The changelog entry sits under **Unreleased**. Whichever of #20 and this merges second combines the two Unreleased entries.

## SDK status against this (dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf main)

| SDK | `eddsa-jcs-2022` (MUST) | `ecdsa-jcs-2019` (SHOULD) |
|---|---|---|
| TypeScript proof | yes | yes |
| Dart proof | yes | yes |
| Go proof | yes | yes |
| Rust `trust-tasks-proof` | yes | **no** (follow-up) |

None of the SDKs implement the pinned PQC suites yet. TDK's `affinidi-data-integrity` implements both under its `post-quantum` feature.

title: fix(sdk): VTA_ALLOW_PRIVATE_ENDPOINTS on the login handshake and session hub
body:
## Problem

`challenge_response` and `SessionHub::new` built their TDK from
`TDKConfig::builder()` with no resolver. The TDK then constructs its own
`DIDCacheClient` from `DIDCacheConfigBuilder::default()`, whose host policy is
`PublicOnly` and which knows nothing about `VTA_ALLOW_PRIVATE_ENDPOINTS`.

Every other resolution in vta-sdk goes through `resolver::webvh_host_policy`, so
an operator running a VTA on a loopback host could opt in everywhere **except**
the one place that packs the authenticate message. Since vta-sdk 0.42
introduced the policy, `did-git-sign` against a local
`did:webvh:…:localhost%3A8100` VTA failed every login, even with the opt-in set:

```
DIDComm pack failed: … Failed to resolve recipient DID: …
BlockedHost: localhost is not a public host (HostPolicy::PublicOnly)
```

## Fix

One crate-private `session_hub::shared_tdk_config()` hands the TDK the
process-shared resolver from `resolver::shared_did_resolver(None)`. Both the
REST authenticate handshake and `SessionHub::new` use it.

- The host policy is now the crate's: `PublicOnly` unless the operator opted in.
- The VTA DID that `resolve_vta_endpoint` fetched a moment earlier answers from
  cache instead of being fetched again.

### Why local mode, not `PNM_RESOLVER_URL`

The keys this resolver finds are the ones messages are encrypted to, and both
paths have always verified the `did:webvh` log in-process rather than on a
sidecar's word. This is the same call, for the same reason, as `didcomm_light`.
Consumers that want a sidecar build their own `TDKConfig` and use
`SessionHub::with_configs`.

## Compatibility

- No public API changes.
- Without the env var, behaviour is unchanged apart from the shared cache
  (300 s, successes only), which the `didcomm_light` auth path already lives with.
- With the env var, these two paths now agree with the rest of the SDK.

## Tests

`session_hub::tests`:

- `shared_tdk_config_carries_the_shared_resolver` — the config never leaves the
  TDK to build its own resolver.
- `opt_in_lets_the_tdk_dial_a_loopback_webvh_host` — re-runs the test binary as
  a child with `VTA_ALLOW_PRIVATE_ENDPOINTS=1` and asserts the TDK's resolver
  dials a loopback `did:webvh` host (counting listener) and does not fail with
  `BlockedHost`. The child runs out of process because the opt-in is read from
  the environment and the shared resolver is cached per policy, so setting it
  in-process would leak into `resolver::tests`, which pin the strict default.

## Verification

```sh
cargo clippy -p vta-sdk --lib --features session -- -D warnings   # clean
cargo test -p vta-sdk --lib --features session session_hub::tests # 8 passed, 1 ignored by design
cargo test -p vta-sdk --lib --features session resolver::tests    # 11 passed
```
