title: Two links 404 on GitHub, and CI does not run the documented markdown lint
body:
Two small things found while reading the developer journey. Both are one PR; happy to send it.

## 1. `developer/01-personal-vta.md` links to `/sysop/…`, which GitHub resolves off the site root

Two links are root-absolute:

```
developer/01-personal-vta.md:4:  **Tested on:** [Ubuntu Server](/sysop/explore/01-server-setup.md)
developer/01-personal-vta.md:96: Complete the [Ubuntu Server](/sysop/explore/01-server-setup.md) deployment before continuing…
```

A leading `/` in rendered markdown resolves against `github.com`, not the repository, so both land on `https://github.com/sysop/explore/01-server-setup.md` — 404 (measured 2026-09-22). Line 96 is in **Prerequisites**, so the first thing the guide asks a developer to do is follow a dead link.

Every other reference in the repo already uses the relative form, including the sibling index:

```
developer/README.md:19:  see [Explore 01 — Server Setup](../sysop/explore/01-server-setup.md) in sysop
sysop/explore/02-walkthrough.md:18:  Complete the [01 — Server setup](01-server-setup.md) first.
```

Fix: `../sysop/explore/01-server-setup.md` in both places. These are the only two broken relative links in the repo — I checked every one.

## 2. `markdownlint-cli2` is configured and documented, but never runs in CI

`CLAUDE.md` names the lint step:

```bash
markdownlint-cli2 "**/*.md"
```

and `.markdownlint.json` is committed (MD013 off, MD024 siblings-only). But `lint.yml` has one job, `shell`, running `shellcheck` and `guard-remote-exec.sh`. Nothing lints the markdown — in a repository whose `CLAUDE.md` opens "a documentation-only repository — no build system, no tests, no application code".

The tree is already clean, so this adds a guard and repairs nothing:

```
$ npx markdownlint-cli2 "**/*.md"
markdownlint-cli2 v0.23.3 (markdownlint v0.41.1)
Linting: 14 files
Summary: 0 issues in 0 files
```

Fix: a `markdown` job in `lint.yml` alongside `shell`, pinned the same way the checkout action already is.

---

Neither of these changes any instruction or any behaviour — link targets and a CI job only. Filing them together because they are both one-line housekeeping; say the word if you would rather have them separate.

title: Explore Step 3 pins release `v1.0.0`, which was never published — the setup script cannot be downloaded
body:
## What happens

`sysop/explore/01-server-setup.md` Step 3 has the operator download `setup-explore.sh` from a tagged release before running it as root:

```bash
VER=v1.0.0
SHA256=c59f53c74f423327a233bb3178651bf7958449efd88df05df8c2f8d179db1340
curl -fsSLO "https://github.com/OpenVTC/vti-setup/releases/download/${VER}/setup-explore.sh"
curl -fsSLO "https://github.com/OpenVTC/vti-setup/releases/download/${VER}/SHA256SUMS"
```

There is no `v1.0.0` release. Both URLs 404, and `-f` makes `curl` exit non-zero, so the operator finishes Step 3 with no script, no `SHA256SUMS`, and no message saying why. The explore stream stops at its first command, and the guide's own instruction — "Do not run a copy from the `main` branch" — leaves no documented way forward.

Measured 2026-09-22:

```
404  https://github.com/OpenVTC/vti-setup/releases/download/v1.0.0/setup-explore.sh
404  https://github.com/OpenVTC/vti-setup/releases/download/v1.0.0/SHA256SUMS
```

Tags on this repository:

| tag | published | assets |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Banyan` | 2026-06-23 | none |
| `archive/sysop-deploy` | — | — |

## The pin is right; the release is missing

This is not a stale hash. `c59f53c7…db1340` is exactly the SHA-256 of `scripts/setup-explore.sh` as it stands on `main`, and the script has not changed since #37 introduced both the verification flow and the pin:

```
$ git show HEAD:scripts/setup-explore.sh | sha256sum
c59f53c74f423327a233bb3178651bf7958449efd88df05df8c2f8d179db1340  -

$ git log --oneline 632747b..HEAD -- scripts/setup-explore.sh
(no output)
```

So `RELEASING.md` step 2 — "Open a PR that sets `VER` and `SHA256` in Step 3 … Merge it." — landed as #37. Step 3, pushing the `v1.0.0` tag that runs `release.yml` and attaches the assets, did not. The guide has been pointing at a release that does not exist since 12 September.

## Why nothing caught it

Nothing checks the pin. `lint.yml` runs `shellcheck` and `guard-remote-exec.sh`; the guard proves no page pipes a download into a shell or fetches from `main`, which is the right property, but it says nothing about whether the pinned release resolves. A guide can therefore instruct a root operator to download from a URL that 404s and every gate in the repo stays green.

Both halves of the verification story are currently unobservable in CI:

- **the pin can drift from the script** — nothing asserts `SHA256` still matches `scripts/setup-explore.sh`, so a future PR touching the script leaves the guide pinning the old hash;
- **the pinned release can be absent** — as it is now.

## Suggested fix

Two parts, only one of which is a code change:

1. **Push the `v1.0.0` tag** so `release.yml` attaches `setup-explore.sh` and `SHA256SUMS` and records the provenance attestation. The hash in the guide is already correct for the current script, so no doc change is needed and `RELEASING.md`'s requirement that the pinning PR not touch the script is satisfied.

2. **Guard the pin in CI**, in the same shape as `guard-remote-exec.sh`, so neither half can go unobserved again. I'll open a PR for this. Two checks on different triggers, because `RELEASING.md` deliberately pins *before* the tag exists:
   - on every pull request — the pinned `SHA256` equals `sha256sum scripts/setup-explore.sh` in the tree under review. This is the drift check, and it passes today.
   - on push to `main` and on a daily schedule — the pinned `VER` release exists and its `setup-explore.sh` asset hashes to the pinned value. This is the check that would have caught the present state, and it will fail until (1) is done.

Splitting the triggers keeps the release-existence check from blocking the pinning PR that `RELEASING.md` asks for, while still turning a never-cut release into a visible failure within a day rather than a silent 404 for a sysop.

Happy to take the guard as a PR; (1) needs a maintainer.

title: fix(vtc)!: admin promotion goes through acl/change-role, behind a step-up
body:
Closes #1645. Resolves the divergence recorded in the VTI specification's
divergence register (Appendix F.2) by trustoverip/dtgwg-vti-spec#35 — that
entry can be closed once this merges.

## Security fix: the step-up on admin promotion was bypassable

**This is the part that matters, and it is not a refactor.**

`vtc/members/update/0.1` carried an in-handler `require_fresh_step_up` for
`role: admin`. That gate bounded one *route*. Two other doors reach the same
ACL row and assign the same `admin` role:

- `acl/change-role/0.1` (`PATCH /v1/acl/{did}`) — `update_acl` set
  `entry.role` and stored it. No step-up, no self-promotion refusal, no
  role-change policy, no VEC re-mint, no serialisation.
- `acl/grant/0.1` (`POST /v1/acl`) — `create_acl` wrote a fresh `admin`
  entry. Same: nothing but `validate_vtc_role_assignment`, which only asks
  whether the *caller* is an admin.

So any admin session could confer admin with no second factor by using the
other door, and the admin console's passkey gesture was decoration rather
than a control. All three claims were verified against the code before
anything was changed.

The gate now sits on the **operation**, not on a route.

### How it is enforced

`role_change_via_pipeline` took a `step_up: bool` from its caller. That made
the handler the gate: the host invariant it fed
(`ceremony::invariant::StepUpForAdmin`) could only check that somebody had
said `true`, and a second route reaching the same row simply said nothing.

The pipeline now resolves the elevation itself, from the caller's **live
session** (`acl::elevation::verified`), and two host invariants are applied
in `ceremony::decide` — around the policy, where an operator's policy edit
cannot reach them:

- `StepUpForAdmin` (**VTI-OPS-051**) — an `allow{role: admin}` needs a live
  elevation.
- `SelfPromotion` (**VTI-OPS-050**, new) — nobody promotes themselves,
  however well authenticated. A second factor proves who is at the keyboard,
  never that a second person agreed.

A vetoed decision is rendered back in its own terms rather than as
`denied by policy (step-up-required)`: the step-up veto answers
`403 step_up_required`, which is the signal the console turns into a passkey
prompt, and the self-promotion veto names the command to run instead.

**`policy.enforcement` (#1633) does not apply here, and nothing depends on
it.** That flag is `vta-config`'s; the VTC has no equivalent. Its decision
pipeline always runs — `load_active_compiled` is not optional, and boot
installs the default bundle idempotently — and `decide` applies the host
invariants unconditionally after the policy. There is no configuration in
which these lapse, and none in which an operator can switch them off by
editing `role_change.rego`.

`acl/grant` is the one gate that is not an invariant, stated plainly rather
than hidden: a grant writes an entry rather than moving one, so there is no
transition to hang one on. It calls the same predicate
(`acl::elevation::verified` / `required`) one layer further out, so the two
cannot drift.

It is gated on the *widening*, not the write (`elevation::
widens_admin_authority`). `acl/grant` is "the entry the maintainer should
hold", so it is also how the console edits an admin's **label** — re-granting
at the same role and the same scopes. Demanding a passkey for that would be
theatre. Demanding it for the rewrite that takes an admin from one context to
two, or from a context to none at all (which is how a community-wide
super-admin is spelled), is not: that is authority conferred without the role
ever changing.

## What came with the promotion, so nothing was lost

Everything the `members/update` path did now happens on `acl/change-role`,
and for every caller of the pipeline rather than for one route:

- **Self-promotion refused** — moved from a handler `if` to the invariant.
- **Serialised** — `PROMOTE_LOCK` moved from `routes/members/update.rs` into
  `ceremony::orchestrate`. The window it closes is a property of the
  operation; with the lock on one handler, the second door raced the first.
- **Compare-and-swap under the lock** — the subject's row is re-read inside
  the critical section and re-checked against the caller's `fromRole`, so a
  promotion racing another role write is a `409` rather than an overwrite of
  whatever landed in between. This subsumes the old already-an-admin
  re-check.
- **Role-change policy + role-VEC re-mint** — the `Remint` executor arm,
  including the no-last-admin guard on demotion that `acl/change-role`
  previously skipped entirely.
- **Admin sister record** — without it a promotion produces an admin who
  cannot enrol a passkey, i.e. cannot sign in to the console.
- **`AdminPromoted` audit** — its own variant beside `AclUpdated`, joined to
  the `AuthSteppedUp` row by `authorisingSessionId`.

`RemintOutcome.role_vec` became `Option<VerifiableCredential>`: a role VEC is
re-minted only where there is a **member row** to repoint it on. An ACL-only
subject (an integration or operator DID, which `acl/change-role` legitimately
serves) has no role assertion to re-issue, and minting one anyway would have
made an ACL role change impossible on a VTC with no credential signer.

## A second escalation, found while moving the promotion

`update_acl` never ran `validate_acl_modification` — `create_acl` always has.
The existing `caller_covers_admin_target` guard only fires on an entry that is
*already* admin, so a context admin of `ctx-a` could not demote a peer admin
scoped to `[ctx-a, ctx-b]` (its own doc comment says so) but **could promote a
member** with those scopes into exactly that entry, minting an admin over a
context they do not hold. The check is now run on the resulting entry, decoded
through `ActScope` so "no scopes" is read as *unrestricted* under `admin` and
*nowhere* under every other role rather than conflated. Covered by
`a_context_admin_cannot_promote_across_a_context_it_does_not_hold`.

## `vtc/members/update` answers `adminRoleForbidden`

`role: admin` is refused with the code the specification declares for it,
using `TaskError::declared` and the generated constant, before anything is
read or written — the task's consumer conformance is "return
`adminRoleForbidden` and change nothing". The message names the replacement
endpoint and body verbatim, per the workspace rule that an operator error
suggests the fix.

Census (`trust_tasks/error_code_census.rs`): witness added,
`s::members::update::v0_1::error_codes::ADMIN_ROLE_FORBIDDEN` removed from
the baseline, `UNWITNESSED` 12 → 11.

## The open question: does `acl/grant` of `admin` count as promotion?

**Decided: no — `acl/grant` cannot promote a member, and that is now
structural rather than incidental.**

A VTC member is 1:1 with an ACL row by DID, and `create_acl` already refuses
a grant that would change an existing entry's role, pointing at
`acl/change-role`. So the only member-facing path to `admin` is the ceremony,
which is where the invariants live. What `acl/grant` can do is *create* an
admin from nothing, or *re-grant* an existing admin (which rewrites its
scopes). Creating one always takes the fresh step-up; re-granting takes it
when the rewrite widens what the entry holds. A self-targeted grant that would
mint the caller a *new* admin entry is refused outright.

The case deliberately **not** gated is a re-grant that confers nothing new —
same role, same scopes. That is how the console corrects a label, and it hands
over no authority that was not already there.

## Affected clients — breaking

| Client | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| `admin-ui` `members.tsx::promoteToAdmin` | passkey step-up, then `PATCH /v1/members/{did}` `{role:"admin"}` under `vtc/members/update/0.1` | passkey step-up (unchanged), then `PATCH /v1/acl/{did}` `{fromRole, toRole:"admin"}` under `acl/change-role/0.1`. `fromRole` comes from the rendered row and is a real compare-and-swap. **Updated in this PR.** |
| `admin-ui` `acl.tsx::createAcl` (**Access control → Add entry**) | no step-up — this was the second half of the bypass, reachable from the console itself | steps up when the role is `admin`, and the form says so before you submit. **Updated in this PR.** |
| Any external client promoting via `members/update` | `200` | `400 adminRoleForbidden`, message naming the replacement |
| Any client conferring `admin` via `acl/change-role` or `acl/grant` **without** a step-up | `200`/`201` | `403 step_up_required` — this is the fix |

The step-up ceremony moved out of `members.tsx` into `lib/step-up.ts` so both
console paths run one implementation — the daemon's gate is shared, so the
client's should be too, and a screen that offers an admin-conferring operation
without it can only ever answer `step_up_required`.

Checked and **not** affected: `vtc-client` has no role-change or promote
function at all (`update_member_extensions` hard-codes an extensions-only
body and cannot send a role); `cnm-cli` has no VTC member-role command — its
`--role admin` surfaces are VTA ACL entries and error-message text. No change
needed in either; neither has a step-up helper, so neither could have
completed a promotion.

## Operational note: what an operator with no passkey can still do

A step-up is `auth/passkey/login/{start,finish}/0.2` with `purpose: stepUp`,
so an admin with no enrolled passkey cannot perform one. That was already
true of the `members/update` promotion, so nothing regresses — but it now
also holds for `acl/change-role` and `acl/grant` of `admin`, which is the
point. First-admin provisioning does not go through either (it is `vtc
setup` / the install token / emergency bootstrap), and the offline
break-glass — `vtc --config <config.toml> acl add --did … --role admin`,
direct fjall with the daemon stopped — is untouched.

## A note on ACL narrowing (#1279, #1619, #1642)

On the VTA an entry can hold less than its role, so a role is a ceiling and a
gate reading only the role over-trusts the entry. Two questions follow for any
promotion gate: what happens to a narrowed capability set when the role moves,
and whether a caller can escalate by widening their own set without touching
their role.

Neither arises here, structurally rather than by luck: `VtcAclEntry` has **no**
`capabilities` field and `AuthClaims` carries none, so a VTC entry is exactly
`(role, scopes)` and nothing can disagree with the role because nothing else is
stored. The analogous widening axis is `scopes`, and `validate_acl_modification`
already bounds it (a non-super-admin cannot confer the unrestricted entry; a
context admin is bounded to contexts it holds). What it does *not* bound is how
recently the caller authenticated — which is why the step-up is required on a
**re-grant that widens**, not only on a fresh one. This is recorded in
`acl/elevation.rs` so that if the VTC ever gains per-entry narrowing, the note
says what has to be decided with it.

## Docs

- `docs/03-vtc/bootstrap-runbook.md` — a new **Adding a second admin later**
  section (both paths, the compare-and-swap, why `members/update` is not it,
  and the no-self-promotion rule), and the existing "Access control → Add
  entry" instruction now says it asks for a passkey.
- `docs/05-design-notes/vtc-mvp.md` §10.4 — the superseded-status note records
  the second move and why the first was not enough.

## Tests

- `ceremony::invariant` — self-promotion vetoed even with a step-up; a
  self-*demotion* still passes; step-up veto unchanged.
- `ceremony::orchestrate` — promotion without a live elevation is
  `StepUpRequired`; self-promotion is `Forbidden` and names the fix; a stale
  `current_role` is a `409`; the happy path and the deny-policy path still
  hold.
- `tests/acl_canonical.rs` (named for the requirements they hold) —
  `vti_ops_051_change_role_to_admin_without_a_live_step_up_is_refused`,
  `vti_ops_051_a_lapsed_step_up_does_not_promote`,
  `vti_ops_051_a_live_step_up_promotes_and_runs_the_role_change_pipeline`
  (asserts the ACL move, the re-minted role VEC, and the admin sister
  record), `vti_ops_050_self_promotion_is_refused_on_the_change_role_path`,
  `vti_ops_051_granting_the_admin_role_without_a_step_up_is_refused`,
  `granting_the_admin_role_with_a_step_up_succeeds`,
  `vti_ops_050_granting_yourself_the_admin_role_is_refused`,
  `re_granting_an_admin_at_the_same_scopes_needs_no_step_up` (and that
  widening the same entry *is* refused),
  `a_context_admin_cannot_promote_across_a_context_it_does_not_hold`, plus two
  regressions that a non-admin role change and a non-admin grant need no
  step-up.
- `tests/members_crud.rs` —
  `the_update_task_answers_with_the_admin_role_forbidden_code_its_spec_declares`
  (the census witness; refused even *with* a live elevation, because it is the
  field that is forbidden) and
  `admin_role_forbidden_is_answered_before_the_member_is_looked_up`.
- `tests/passkey_step_up.rs` — `a_step_up_authorises_the_promotion_it_was_run_for`
  retargeted at `acl/change-role`, so the end-to-end WebAuthn ceremony still
  covers the operation it authorises.

title: vtc: admin promotion goes through members/update, which declares adminRoleForbidden; acl/change-role promotes with no step-up (VTI-OPS-110/051)
body:
Tracks the intended resolution of a divergence recorded in the VTI specification's divergence register (Appendix F.2) by trustoverip/dtgwg-vti-spec#35. Found while building #1644, which left `vtc/members/update:adminRoleForbidden` on the unwitnessed baseline in `vtc-service/src/trust_tasks/error_code_census.rs`.

## What the definition says

`specs/vtc/members/update/0.1` in dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf declares `adminRoleForbidden` ("`role` was `admin`. Promotion to admin is a separate, gated flow, not a metadata update."), its payload schema says `role` MUST NOT be `admin`, and its consumer conformance says: if `role` is `admin`, return `adminRoleForbidden` and change nothing.

`specs/acl/change-role/0.1` is the task defined for role transitions. It says maintainers MAY require stronger authentication, such as a passkey step-up, for a transition into an elevated role, and SHOULD forbid self-promotion.

## What vtc-service does

- `routes/members/update.rs::update_member` accepts `role: admin`. It refuses self-promotion, requires `require_fresh_step_up` in the handler, serialises on `PROMOTE_LOCK`, and runs the role-change pipeline (`role_change.rego`, which re-mints the role VEC). `adminRoleForbidden` is never emitted.
- The admin console relies on this path. `admin-ui/src/plugins/members.tsx::promoteToAdmin` runs `auth/passkey/login/{start,finish}/0.2` with `purpose: stepUp`, then sends `PATCH /v1/members/{did}` `{role: "admin"}` under `vtc/members/update/0.1`.
- `routes/acl.rs::update_acl` (`acl/change-role/0.1`) and `create_acl` (`acl/grant/0.1`) both assign `VtcRole::Admin` to any admin caller through `validate_vtc_role_assignment`. Neither requires a step-up or refuses self-promotion, and neither runs the role-change pipeline. **So the step-up on the members/update path does not bound promotion today.** An admin session without a step-up can promote through `acl/change-role` or `acl/grant`.

## Intended resolution

1. Require a fresh step-up on `acl/change-role` (and on `acl/grant` when the role granted is `admin`), as a rule evaluated at the policy gate rather than a check in a handler (VTI-OPS-050/051).
2. Carry over what the members/update path does: refuse self-promotion, serialise against concurrent role writes, and apply the role-change policy and VEC re-mint.
3. Point `promoteToAdmin` in the admin console (and `cnm` / `vtc-client`, if they promote) at `acl/change-role`.
4. Refuse `role: admin` on `vtc/members/update` with `adminRoleForbidden`, and remove it from the census baseline (lower `UNWITNESSED`).
5. Close the Appendix F entry.

Step 1 has to land before step 3. Moving the console first would remove the only gate that promotion has.

title: fix(vtc)!: admin promotion goes through acl/change-role, behind a step-up (#1658)
body:
fix(vtc)!: admin promotion goes through acl/change-role, behind a step-up (#1658)

`vtc/members/update/0.1` carried an in-handler step-up for `role: admin`.
That gate bounded one route. `acl/change-role` and `acl/grant` reach the
same ACL row and assign the same `admin` role, and neither asked for a
step-up, refused self-promotion, or ran the role-change pipeline — so the
gate was walked around by using a different door. The task also *declares*
`adminRoleForbidden` for exactly this: promotion is a separate, gated flow,
not a metadata update.

The gate now sits on the operation. `role_change_via_pipeline` took a
`step_up: bool` from its caller, which made the handler the gate; it now
resolves the elevation from the caller's live session, and two host
invariants are applied around the policy in `ceremony::decide`, where an
operator's policy edit cannot reach them: `StepUpForAdmin` (VTI-OPS-051)
and `SelfPromotion` (VTI-OPS-050, new). The VTC has no `policy.enforcement`
switch and its pipeline always runs, so neither can lapse by configuration.
`acl/grant` of `admin` checks the same predicate directly — it writes an
entry rather than moving one, so there is no transition to hang an invariant
on — and refuses a self-mint.

Everything the members/update path did came with the promotion: the promote
lock moved into the ceremony (the window is a property of the operation, and
with the lock on one handler the second door raced it), the already-an-admin
re-check generalised into a compare-and-swap re-read under that lock, the
role-change policy and role-VEC re-mint, the admin sister record, and the
`AdminPromoted` audit row.

`update_acl` also never ran `validate_acl_modification`. The existing
`caller_covers_admin_target` guard only fires on an entry that is already
admin, so a context admin of ctx-a could not demote a peer scoped to
`[ctx-a, ctx-b]` but could promote a member with those scopes into exactly
that entry. It is checked now, decoded through `ActScope`.

`RemintOutcome.role_vec` is now `Option<VerifiableCredential>`: a role VEC is
re-minted only where there is a member row to repoint it on, so an ACL-only
subject no longer needs a credential signer to change role.

Breaking: a client promoting via `PATCH /v1/members/{did}` `{role:"admin"}`
now gets `400 adminRoleForbidden` naming the replacement, and conferring
`admin` through `acl/change-role` or `acl/grant` without a live elevation
now gets `403 step_up_required`. The admin console is updated here; it was
the only client in the repo that promoted. `vtc-client` and `cnm-cli` have
no promotion path.

Closes #1645. Resolves the divergence register entry in
trustoverip/dtgwg-vti-spec#35 (Appendix F.2).

title: fix(vtc): refuse an invalid claimSchema at registration, and name the broken type at issuance
body:
Refs #1649, #1600

#1649 made `vtc/endorsements/issue/0.1` enforce the endorsement type's stored
`claimSchema`, which registration had always stored and nothing had ever read.
That turned a document nobody had validated into a load-bearing one: a type
registered with a `claimSchema` that is not itself valid JSON Schema now fails
**every** issuance against it with a 500, and neither the issuer (whose claim is
fine) nor the operator (who sees "internal error") can tell why.

Both ends are fixed. The schema is checked where it is supplied, and where a
pre-existing broken one is met the answer says the *type* is broken.

## At registration — refused, naming the bad keyword

`POST /v1/endorsement-types` now refuses a `claimSchema` that will not compile,
with the part of the document that is wrong:

```
400 {"error":"claimSchema is not a valid JSON Schema — at /properties/level/type:
     \"intiger\" is not valid under any of the schemas listed in the 'anyOf' keyword.
     Correct the schema and register again; …",
     "code":"malformedRequest"}
```

**No declared code covers it.** `vtc/endorsement-types/register/0.1` declares
exactly three — `invalidUri`, `reserved`, `exists` — and `invalidUri` is "empty
or over 512 bytes", about `typeUri`. So the refusal carries the framework's
standard `malformedRequest` (SPEC §8.3), spelled
`trust_tasks_rs::StandardCode::MalformedRequest.as_str()`, not a literal and not
a new code minted under the task's namespace.

**The census baseline is unchanged (still 12).** The census tracks the codes a
`spec/vtc/*` task *declares*; all five endorsement-type/endorsement codes in
scope were already witnessed by #1649, and `CONSUMER_MINTED` is for codes
namespaced under the task slug, which a framework code is not. `TaskError`'s
doc comment is updated to say the standard-code case is allowed, so the "always
a generated constant" invariant stays honest.

**There is no update or upsert path.** The endorsement-type surface is
register / list / delete only, so register is the one gate.

The check is `crate::schemas::check_schema`, which makes the *same*
`jsonschema::validator_for` call `validate_instance` makes at issuance — so a
schema registration accepts is one issuance can use, and one it refuses is one
issuance would choke on. A separate, stricter gate would only move the failure
to a different pair of inputs. A non-object is refused before the compile:
`claimSchema` is `"type": "object"` in the register payload schema, while JSON
Schema itself accepts the bare booleans as schemas.

## At issuance — a 5xx that names the type, not the claim

A stored schema that will not compile is answered with a 500 whose message
names the type and says what to do:

```
500 {"error":"endorsement type 'https://…/corrupt' has an invalid stored
     claimSchema (at /type: \"intiger\" is not valid …) — the claim was not at
     fault. An admin must delete and re-register the type with a valid JSON
     Schema before it can be issued against."}
```

It carries **no** `code`, and deliberately not `claimSchemaViolation`: that code
means a claim failed a *valid* schema and would send the operator to fix the
claim, which is the one thing that is not wrong. No other declared code fits
either, and a 4xx would blame the caller for server-side state. The type id is
logged at `error!` alongside the compile detail.

## Existing data — one WARN per broken type at boot

`report_invalid_claim_schemas` walks the registry at boot and logs one WARN per
type whose stored `claimSchema` will not compile, naming the type, the bad part
and the fix. Same shape as #1633's unenforced-policy warning: advisory, a read
failure is logged and never stops boot. It was cheap — `all_types` plus the same
`check_schema` — so it is here rather than in the PR body as a reason not to.

## Consumers

- **admin-ui**: `StatementTypesCard` sends only `typeUri` and `description` —
  it never sends `claimSchema`, so its register call cannot be refused where it
  was not before. If it ever does, the card already renders the daemon's message
  verbatim (`errorMessage(register.error)`). No UI code change.
- **`openapi.json` is regenerated, description-only, and it is a correctness
  fix.** `claimSchema`'s doc comment is rendered into the document, and the one
  checked in still said the schema was "reserved for future per-type validation"
  and that issuance "only checks type is registered without consulting the
  schema" — which #1649 made false. The new text is two lines, so the field's
  history moved into an ordinary `//` comment that utoipa does not read.
  `wire.ts` regenerates byte-identical (openapi-typescript drops a description
  sitting beside a `$ref`), and `npm run lint`'s `wire:check` confirms it.
- **vtc-client**: does not touch endorsement types.
- No REST body or status changed, and no `#[utoipa::path]` was touched. The 400
  gains a `code` member exactly as every other declared refusal on this route
  already does.

## Tests

- `check_schema_names_the_part_that_is_not_a_schema`,
  `check_schema_refuses_a_non_object` (unit) — a valid schema compiles; four
  malformed ones each report their JSON Pointer; the four non-object shapes are
  named.
- `a_claim_schema_that_is_not_a_json_schema_is_refused_at_registration` — 400 +
  `malformedRequest` + the bad part in the message, nothing stored, and the same
  URI registers once the schema is a schema. A type with no `claimSchema` is
  unaffected.
- `a_type_with_a_corrupt_stored_claim_schema_names_the_type_not_the_claim` — the
  corrupt row is written straight into the keyspace (the fixed registration path
  cannot produce one), issuance answers 500 naming the type with no error code,
  nothing is issued, and delete-then-re-register restores issuance.
- `all_types_returns_every_row_in_key_order` — the new storage helper.
- `a_claim_failing_the_type_claim_schema_is_the_declared_violation` is unchanged
  and still green: a valid schema still passes a good claim and still refuses a
  bad one with `claimSchemaViolation`.

## Noted, not fixed

`jsonschema`'s default features include `resolve-http` and `resolve-file`, so
compiling a schema with an external `$ref` can make a blocking fetch. That is
pre-existing on the issuance path (`validate_instance` has always done it, for
`credentialSchema` as well as `claimSchema`), reachable by the same admin, and
turning it off is a workspace-wide dependency change — out of scope here, worth
a follow-up.

## Verification

- `cargo test -p vtc-service -p vtc-client --no-fail-fast` — 67 binaries, **1836
  passed, 0 failed** (run on the rebased tree, `VTC_SKIP_ADMIN_UI_BUILD` unset).
- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings` — clean.
- `cargo fmt --all -- --check` — clean.
- admin-ui `npm run lint` + `npx vitest run` — 21 files, 170 tests, all pass.

body:
### Specifications

- **messaging/account**: Opt-in activity timestamps on account/get and account/list ([#594](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/pull/594))

Account gains optional lastReceivedAt (the last message accepted for it,
  may lag by up to 60 s) and lastAuthenticatedAt (its last completed
  authentication), both Unix epoch seconds. A mediator returns them only
  when the request sets includeActivity: generated clients reject unknown
  members, so a requester that did not ask must never see them.

title: chore(release): 0.11.0
body:
Cuts **0.11.0**, the first release published to crates.io since 0.9.1.

## Why 0.11.0 and not 0.10.0

`Cargo.toml` has said 0.10.0 since #28, and the CHANGELOG has a `[0.10.0] - 2026-09-11` section, but no `v0.10.0` tag was ever pushed, so 0.10.0 never reached crates.io (latest there is 0.9.1). Since then #31 (`feat!`, `taskDigestMultibase`) merged, and its code already carries `#[deprecated(since = "0.11.0")]`. So this releases both as 0.11.0 rather than retroactively tagging 0.10.0.

## Changes

- `Cargo.toml`: `0.10.0` → `0.11.0`
- `CHANGELOG.md`:
  - `[Unreleased]` content moves under `## [0.11.0] - 2026-09-22`, with `[Unreleased]` left empty
  - a lead paragraph and an **Upgrading from 0.9** section for consumers crossing 0.10.0 and 0.11.0 at once: `DTGCredentialError` is `#[non_exhaustive]` (+9 variants), `new_member_vmc` / `new_delegate_vdc` / `new_vwc` deprecated in favour of `new_member_vmc_for` / `new_delegate_vdc_for` / `new_vwc_for_session`, and `DTGCommon::task_digest_multibase` breaks exhaustive struct literals. Ordering: verifiers first (from 0.10.0's stricter checks); 0.11.0 adds none.
  - the `[0.10.0]` section is marked **never published to crates.io**
- `README.md`: the upgrade-ordering table gains a 0.11.0 row ("Any order") and notes that 0.10.0 first ships in 0.11.0

No code changes. The file has no compare links, so none to update.

## affinidi-tdk bump (#30)

Not user-visible: `affinidi-tdk` (0.12 → 0.16) is a **dev-dependency** only (examples and integration tests), so no CHANGELOG entry. The affinidi crates that *are* in the public API (`affinidi-data-integrity` 0.7: `DataIntegrityProof`, `DataIntegrityError` via `#[from]`; `affinidi-secrets-resolver` 0.5: `&Secret` in `sign`) are unchanged since 0.9.1.

## Verification (local, on this commit)

- `cargo fmt --check`: clean
- `cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings`, `--all-features` and `--no-default-features`: clean
- `cargo test --all-features`: 186 passed, 0 failed
- `cargo test --no-default-features`: 170 passed, 0 failed
- `cargo doc --no-deps`, both feature sets: builds
- `cargo publish --dry-run --locked`: packaged 23 files (561.9 KiB, 140.0 KiB compressed), verify build OK, upload aborted (dry run)

Pre-existing, not addressed here: `RUSTDOCFLAGS="-D warnings" cargo doc --no-default-features` fails on intra-doc links to `DTGCredential::sign` / `verify_proof_with_public_key`, which only exist behind `affinidi-signing`. docs.rs builds default features, and CI does not run rustdoc, so it does not block the release.

## Publishing (after merge — not done in this PR)

Earlier release tags (`v0.9.0`, `v0.9.1`) are **annotated, not signed**, on the merge commit, with a `vX.Y.Z — <summary>` message. To match:

```sh
git fetch origin
MERGE_SHA=$(git rev-parse origin/main)   # confirm this is the squash-merge of this PR
```

title: spec(messaging/account): opt-in activity timestamps on account/get and account/list
body:
## What

Two optional members on the shared `Account` record, so an operator can see when each account was last active:

- `lastReceivedAt`: Unix epoch seconds when the mediator last accepted a message addressed to the account. It may lag by up to 60 seconds, so a mediator can throttle the write instead of adding one to every message.
- `lastAuthenticatedAt`: Unix epoch seconds when the account last completed authentication, over any transport.

Both use epoch seconds, like `AuditEntry.timestamp`.

## Why opt-in

`account/get` and `account/list` each gain an optional request member, `includeActivity`. A mediator returns the timestamps only when it is `true`, and **MUST NOT** otherwise.

The generated clients reject unknown members (`deny_unknown_fields` in Rust, `additionalProperties: false` in the schema). A mediator that always sent the new members would break every existing requester that parses these responses. With the flag, older requesters never see them.

In the other direction, a requester that sends `includeActivity` to an older mediator gets a schema rejection. The prose says a requester **SHOULD** set it only where it knows the mediator supports it.

The change is additive inside version 0.1 of `messaging/account/{get,list}`: every existing document stays valid.

## Also

- Security & Privacy notes for both tasks: these timestamps are a behavioural signal beyond the account's configuration, so they get the same authorization as the rest of the account view.
- All four client libraries regenerated (Rust, TS, Go, Dart). `npm run build`, `npm run check-bindings` and `cargo test -p trust-tasks-rs` pass.

title: vta-service-v0.39.0
body:
### Added

- **backup**: A backup is the whole agent, and restores between plain, hardened and TEE VTAs ([#1655](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1655))

A backup now carries every row of every keyspace in vta_keyspaces::BACKED_UP
  (format vta-backup-v2) and restores into a plain, hardened or Nitro-enclave
  VTA from any of them. VTI-VTA-001, VTI-VTA-050, VTI-VTA-051, VTI-KEY-033.

- **persona**: Wear a face here without naming a persona DID ([#1654](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1654))

Implements trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf#589 (design note
  persona-context-first.md §9.7).

  binding/set takes an omitted `personaDid`, and profile/compose takes
  `wear: true`: the agent uses the persona the holder already uses in the
  context — the one DID with a binding record there, current or cleared —
  and names it in the response. None is refused (`noPersonaHere`),
  several are refused (`personaAmbiguous`, naming them), and compose
  refuses `wear` beside a `personaDid` (`wearAndPersona`). Neither task
  mints a persona: a DID has a lifecycle of its own, and a write that could
  half-create one would leave a published identity nobody holds.



### Fixed

- **persona**: A credential-backed value follows its credential, and fails closed ([#1653](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1653))

Credential-backed attributes were never resolved against their
  credential: not at write (persona/attribute/put rule 3,
  `credentialNotFound`) and, worse, not on read, where the Provenance
  contract requires the maintainer to re-derive the value and fail closed
  once the credential is revoked, expired, archived or deleted. A revoked
  credential's value went on being presented.

  vta-persona gains `derive`: a `CredentialSource` hook the service
  implements over the vault, so the persona crate still does not depend
  on it. The store asks it wherever a credential-backed value is about to
  be believed:
  - put: resolves the credential and takes its value (the supplied one is
    a display cache the spec lets the maintainer overwrite); one it cannot
    back is refused. `credential_refusal` gives the dispatcher the code.
  - resolving a face (and so materialising a binding): the credential's
    current value, or nothing and `stale`.
  - listing the pool: `stale` with `staleReason`, no value; a withheld
    value stays withheld.
  - building a preview: re-derived from the context's copy, which carries
    the provenance; a withdrawn credential shows stale before approval.
  - presenting: checked again, so a credential revoked between preview
    and present is not presented.
  A pinned kept value is withheld too once its credential is withdrawn.

  vta-vault `receive::stored_claims`: the claims a stored credential
  carries — SD-JWT-VC re-verified against its issuer and reconstructed,
  Data-Integrity read as stored, mdoc refused. vta-service's
  `VaultCredentials` maps held/lifecycle/status/validity window/path to a
  value or a StaleReason; attribute/put maps a refusal to
  `persona/attribute/put:credentialNotFound`, and reads the stored value
  back for its correlation count.

- **auth**: A signed REST sign-in must be addressed to the service that receives it ([#1646](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1646))

title: vti-common-v0.23.0
body:
### Added

- **backup**: A backup is the whole agent, and restores between plain, hardened and TEE VTAs ([#1655](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1655))

A backup now carries every row of every keyspace in vta_keyspaces::BACKED_UP
  (format vta-backup-v2) and restores into a plain, hardened or Nitro-enclave
  VTA from any of them. VTI-VTA-001, VTI-VTA-050, VTI-VTA-051, VTI-KEY-033.

- **vtc**: Deliver an invitation to the DID it admits — pushed as an offer, or as a QR ([#1648](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1648))

Keyring VTI-21 and VTI-32. `vtc/invitations/issue` returned the signed
  invitation to the inviter once and nothing carried it further, and the
  credential was too large for a QR code (the console said so).

  `vtc/invitations/deliver/0.1` (`POST /v1/invitations/deliver`, inviter
  roles) records a single-use OID4VCI offer for the invitation, bound to the
  invited DID and withdrawing any earlier one, then either sends it to that
  DID as a `credential-exchange/offer` over DIDComm (`message`; `noRoute`,
  422, when the DID advertises no DIDComm service) or returns it (`offer`).
  The offer names the credential rather than containing it, so it fits a QR
  code as an `openid-credential-offer://` link.

  The invitation is released only through `credential-exchange/request` with
  a key-binding proof by the invited DID's key, so a photographed code admits
  no one else. Two things that required:

  - Key-binding proofs now verify for a holder of any DID method: the `kid`
    resolves through the community's DID resolver (`DidVmResolver`), where
    the verifier refused anything but a `did:key`. `redeem` and
    `issue_on_request` take the resolver.
  - `POST /v1/credential-exchange/request` redeems over HTTPS, for an invitee
    with no messaging service. Unauthenticated, on the rate-limited unauth
    chain: the proof is the authority. It answers with the
    `credential-exchange/issue` payload a messaging binding sends on-thread.

  The signed invitation is kept on its registry row so it can be delivered
  later (never listed). Invitations issued before this cannot be delivered
  and say to reissue. The admin console gets Send and QR-offer buttons on
  each live invitation. AuditEvent::InvitationDelivered.



### Fixed

- **auth**: A signed REST sign-in must be addressed to the service that receives it ([#1646](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1646))

title: Give each requirement area its own chapter, and make Appendix E's record form normative
body:
Closes #32.

This works through the six findings of the structural review. No requirement's text or identifier changes.

| # | Finding | Disposition |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Trust Contexts chapter bundles four areas | **Split** into Trust Contexts (`CTX`, 17), Access Control and Authority (`ACL`, 43), Approvals, Consent and Step-Up (`APV`, 14) and Audit (`AUD`, 6): `03-trust-contexts.md` and `03a`–`03c`. All 80 requirements move verbatim. Cross-references are updated throughout, including the Core profile and the reading guide. |
| 2 | Appendix E informative, but CMP-002/CMP-120 rely on it | **New normative E.1 "Record form"**: the fields of a record and the ownership vocabulary. Evidence families (E.2) and assessment submissions (E.3) stay informative. CMP-002 and CMP-120 now point at E.1. A note on CNF-006 says it binds the spec and its test suite, not any target (per CNF-001). |
| 3 | VTC material split across three files | The VTC chapter now points to the Membership Lifecycle and Trust Registries chapters. The reading-guide row for a VTC names all three. |
| 4 | Only sibling spec split per chapter | **Kept.** `STRUCTURE.md` now records it as a deliberate choice, along with the three places the chapter list must stay in sync. |
| 5 | `11a-vtn.md` lettered filename | **Not renumbered**, per the existing decision in `STRUCTURE.md`. The new `03a`–`03c` follow the same convention, and filenames are not identifiers. |
| 6 | SES-042 after SES-043 | Moved into order. |

### For reviewers

- The "In plain terms" intros for **Approvals, Consent and Step-Up** and **Audit** are new text. The other two reuse the old chapter's intro, divided between them.
- Document Status stays at `0.1.0`, because no requirement's substance changed.
- The comma in "Approvals, Consent and Step-Up" renders as an `approvals%2C-consent-and-step-up` anchor. Nothing links to it yet.

title: Structural review: split Trust Contexts chapter, tighten Appendix E normativity, VTC cross-references
body:
## Summary

Structural review of the VTI spec (all 22 chapter files, ~4500 lines), done as the "review the VTI spec structure and suggest improvements if needed" action item. This is a structural review only — not a line-level correctness pass — and it also checked chapter organization against the sibling DTGWG specs (Credentials, Trust Tasks) for consistency.

**Overall verdict:** the structure is basically sound. The four-part organization (Foundations / Common Model / Nodes / System Properties) is coherent, the reading-guide table in the introduction is accurate, chapter ordering respects dependencies (contexts and authority before the things built on them, nodes after the common model, composition/operations last), and the ending convention (Considerations → Conformance → References → Appendix) matches both sibling specs exactly. No deeper reorganization is warranted. One finding below is worth real effort; the rest are small, targeted fixes.

## Findings

### 1. Split `03-trust-contexts.md` (626 lines) — it bundles four requirement areas into one chapter

The Conformance chapter's own area table treats `CTX`, `ACL`, `APV` (approvals/consent/step-up), and `AUD` (audit) as four separate requirement areas — exactly like every other area in the document gets its own chapter (`KEY`→04, `TRN`→05, `SES`→06, `CLT`→07, …). But all four currently live in one file titled "Trust Contexts and the Authority Model," which doesn't mention approvals or audit in its title and is 2–8x longer than any sibling chapter. A reader looking for step-up/consent rules or audit requirements has no reason to look here.

**Suggested fix:** split into at least four chapters matching the four requirement areas — Trust Contexts (`CTX`), Access Control and Authority (`ACL`), Approvals/Consent/Step-Up (`APV`), Audit (`AUD`) — consistent with how every other area in the document is organized.

### 2. Appendix E is labeled informative but two MUST requirements depend on it

VTI-CMP-002 requires a conformance claim to state evidence "recorded in Appendix E"; VTI-CMP-120 requires ownership classification/evidence/counter-cases to be recorded there. Both are normative obligations pointing at a section the document marks "This appendix is informative."

**Suggested fix:** either promote the specific record format to normative, or rephrase CMP-002/CMP-120 to point at a normative subsection rather than the whole appendix.

Related, flagging alongside rather than as a separate ask: VTI-CNF-006 requires every requirement to map to a conformance test, but `95-conformance.md` admits the test suite's location "is not yet settled" — a MUST resting on infrastructure that doesn't exist yet.

### 3. `11-vtc.md` (81 lines) is thin, and VTC's content is split across three files with no cross-pointer

VTA gets 166 lines; VTN — which has zero implementations and an explicitly open structural question — gets 304. VTC, one of only two node types with real implementations, has its real content split across `11-vtc.md`, `12-vtc-lifecycle.md`, and `13-registries.md`, with no forward-pointer between them. A reader following the "Implementing or operating a VTC" row in the intro's reading-guide table has to independently discover it needs all three.

**Suggested fix:** add a one-line "see also" at the top of `11-vtc.md` pointing to 12 and 13.

### 4. VTI is the only one of the three sibling specs split into per-chapter files

`dtgwg-cred-spec` and `dtgwg-trust-tasks-spec` each use a single `body.md`; VTI uses ~20 numbered files. Defensible given VTI's size (4500 vs. 600–1400 lines), but it means the intro's "Structure of this document" table and `specs.json`'s `markdown_paths` list are two places that must stay in sync as chapters move — a maintenance mode the siblings don't have.

**Suggested fix:** no code change needed — just worth this being a deliberate, acknowledged choice rather than an unexamined one. Flagging for awareness.

### 5. `11a-vtn.md` is the only lettered filename in an otherwise sequential scheme

Evidently VTN was inserted after 02–15 were already numbered. Harmless — chapter file numbers aren't the stable identifiers, `VTI-XXX-nnn` requirement IDs are, and those don't reference file numbers — but a small renumbering (VTN→12, shifting Membership/Registries/Composition/Operational down one) would remove the only rough edge in the numbering.

### 6. `VTI-SES-042` is defined out of order in `06-sessions-auth.md`

It appears after `VTI-SES-043` in the text. Cosmetic, but the document repeatedly states that identifiers are "allocated in order within its area," so this is a small inconsistency with its own stated convention.

## Priority

Finding 1 is the only one worth real effort. Findings 2 and 3 are quick, targeted fixes. Finding 4 is informational (no action needed unless the WG wants to reconsider the file-split approach). Findings 5 and 6 are cosmetic and can be batched into any of the other fixes' PRs.

title: Give each requirement area its own chapter, and make Appendix E's record form normative (#36)
body:
Give each requirement area its own chapter, and make Appendix E's record form normative (#36)

* Give each requirement area its own chapter, and make Appendix E's record form normative

Addresses the structural review in #32.

The Trust Contexts chapter carried four requirement areas under one
title. It is split along them: Trust Contexts (CTX), Access Control and
Authority (ACL), Approvals, Consent and Step-Up (APV), and Audit (AUD),
in 03-trust-contexts.md and 03a-03c. Every requirement moves verbatim
and keeps its identifier. Each new chapter opens with the plain-terms
and scope sections the others carry. Every cross-reference to the old
chapter now names the chapter that holds the requirement: specs.json,
the intro's structure and reading-guide tables, the Core profile and
area tables, and the architecture walkthrough, Clients, Operations,
VTC, VTN, Composition and Appendix B.

VTI-CMP-002 and VTI-CMP-120 pointed at an appendix marked informative.
Appendix E now has a normative E.1 that fixes the record form and the
ownership vocabulary, and both requirements point at it. The evidence
families (E.2) and assessment submissions (E.3) stay informative. A note
on VTI-CNF-006 says it binds the specification and its test suite, not
any conformance target.

The VTC chapter points to the Membership Lifecycle and Trust Registries
chapters, and the reading guide names all three. VTI-SES-042 now comes
before VTI-SES-043.

STRUCTURE.md records the one-file-per-chapter choice as a deliberate
departure from the sibling specs, and the three places a chapter list
must be kept in sync. It also records one requirement area per chapter.
The suffixed filenames stay: renumbering would cost file history, and
filenames are not identifiers.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* Add Audit to the VTC reading-guide row

The VTA row lists all four split chapters (Trust contexts, Access
control and authority, Approvals/consent/step-up, Audit); the VTC row
dropped Audit, even though VTC administration is subject to the same
ACL/APV model (VTI-VTC-020/021) and audit events apply to VTC activity
too.

Signed-off-by: Brendan A. Miller <code+os@brendanmiller.com>

* Add editors and contributors, bump Document Status to 0.2.0

Add Alberto Leon, Brendan A. Miller, and Drummond Reed as editors
(alphabetical, alongside Glenn Gore), and Sankarshan Mukhopadhyay and
the DTGWG participants as contributors.

Signed-off-by: Brendan A. Miller <code+os@brendanmiller.com>

* Note the DCO requirement for source code contributions in README

Per the DTGWG's Joint Development Foundation charter, source code
contributions are subject to Developer Certificate of Origin v1.1;
this wasn't documented anywhere in the repository.

## `vta-sdk`

## [0.49.0](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/compare/vta-sdk-v0.48.0...vta-sdk-v0.49.0) — 2026-09-22 ### Added - **backup**: A backup is the whole agent, and restores between plain, hardened and TEE VTAs ([#1655](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1655)) A backup now carries every row of every keyspace in vta_keyspaces::BACKED_UP (format vta-backup-v2) and restores into a plain, hardened or Nitro-enclave VTA from any of them. VTI-VTA-001, VTI-VTA-050, VTI-VTA-051, VTI-KEY-033. - **persona**: Wear a face here without naming a persona DID ([#1654](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1654)) Implements trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf#589 (design note persona-context-first.md §9.7). binding/set takes an omitted `personaDid`, and profile/compose takes `wear: true`: the agent uses the persona the holder already uses in the context — the one DID with a binding record there, current or cleared — and names it in the response. None is refused (`noPersonaHere`), several are refused (`personaAmbiguous`, naming them), and compose refuses `wear` beside a `personaDid` (`wearAndPersona`). Neither task mints a persona: a DID has a lifecycle of its own, and a write that could half-create one would leave a published identity nobody holds. - **vtc**: Deliver an invitation to the DID it admits — pushed as an offer, or as a QR ([#1648](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1648)) Keyring VTI-21 and VTI-32. `vtc/invitations/issue` returned the signed invitation to the inviter once and nothing carried it further, and the credential was too large for a QR code (the console said so). `vtc/invitations/deliver/0.1` (`POST /v1/invitations/deliver`, inviter roles) records a single-use OID4VCI offer for the invitation, bound to the invited DID and withdrawing any earlier one, then either sends it to that DID as a `credential-exchange/offer` over DIDComm (`message`; `noRoute`, 422, when the DID advertises no DIDComm service) or returns it (`offer`). The offer names the credential rather than containing it, so it fits a QR code as an `openid-credential-offer://` link. The invitation is released only through `credential-exchange/request` with a key-binding proof by the invited DID's key, so a photographed code admits no one else. Two things that required: - Key-binding proofs now verify for a holder of any DID method: the `kid` resolves through the community's DID resolver (`DidVmResolver`), where the verifier refused anything but a `did:key`. `redeem` and `issue_on_request` take the resolver. - `POST /v1/credential-exchange/request` redeems over HTTPS, for an invitee with no messaging service. Unauthenticated, on the rate-limited unauth chain: the proof is the authority. It answers with the `credential-exchange/issue` payload a messaging binding sends on-thread. The signed invitation is kept on its registry row so it can be delivered later (never listed). Invitations issued before this cannot be delivered and say to reissue. The admin console gets Send and QR-offer buttons on each live invitation. AuditEvent::InvitationDelivered.

None is refused (`noPersonaHere`), several are refused (`personaAmbiguous`, naming them), and compose refuses `wear` beside a `personaDid` (`wearAndPersona`). Neither task mints a persona: a DID has a lifecycle of its own, and a write that could half-create one would leave a published identity nobody holds. ### Fixed - **persona**: A credential-backed value follows its credential, and fails closed ([#1653](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1653)) Credential-backed attributes were never resolved against their credential: not at write (persona/attribute/put rule 3, `credentialNotFound`) and, worse, not on read, where the Provenance contract requires the maintainer to re-derive the value and fail closed once the credential is revoked, expired, archived or deleted. A revoked credential's value went on being presented. vta-persona gains `derive`: a `CredentialSource` hook the service implements over the vault, so the persona crate still does not depend on it. The store asks it wherever a credential-backed value is about to be believed: - put: resolves the credential and takes its value (the supplied one is a display cache the spec lets the maintainer overwrite); one it cannot back is refused. `credential_refusal` gives the dispatcher the code. - resolving a face (and so materialising a binding): the credential's current value, or nothing and `stale`. - listing the pool: `stale` with `staleReason`, no value; a withheld value stays withheld. - building a preview: re-derived from the context's copy, which carries the provenance; a withdrawn credential shows stale before approval. - presenting: checked again, so a credential revoked between preview and present is not presented. title: security(auth)!: detect refresh-token reuse and revoke the session it belongs to
body:
Rotation already made a stolen refresh token worth exactly one access token, but it said nothing about the theft. Rotation deletes the live `refresh:` index, so a replayed token and a token this node never issued look identical — both simply absent — and the clearest sign of compromise, a token presented after it was spent, arrived as an ordinary 401 (RFC 9700 §4.14.2).

Every rotation now leaves a `RefreshTombstone` at `rotated:{sha256}`, and a token that misses the live index is checked against it. No tombstone means a plain rejection, as before. A hit means this node issued the token and already spent it — theft, or one specific non-attack.

That non-attack is a client whose rotation response was lost in flight, retrying the only token it holds. Treating it as theft would sign the user out on a dropped connection, so the alarm would fire for the routine fault while a patient attacker never tripped it. A replay is forgiven only when the session is alive, the replay is inside `refresh_reuse_grace` (default 30s; `0` disables the concession), and the tombstoned successor is still unspent — which holds only while the client demonstrably never received the response. The retry re-serves the same pair against the existing `token_id` and does not extend the refresh deadline.

Anything else is reuse: the session is deleted, taking its live refresh index and so every descendant of the replayed token with it, and `AuthAuditEvent::RefreshReuseDetected` fires at `error!` with `security_alert = true` and a triage reason. Both outcomes return the same `RefreshTokenInvalid` a stranger's token gets, so detection is not an oracle for an attacker probing when to stop.

Tombstones hold no bearer secret: the token they describe is the hashed key, and its successor is stored as a hash. They are reaped on time alone by `cleanup_expired_sessions`, at `rotated_at + refresh_token_ttl` — deliberately not alongside their session, since replay after a revocation is the case most worth catching.

The logic lives in the canonical handler, so VTA and VTC both get it. The two new `SessionStore` methods have no-op defaults, so an out-of-tree store keeps exactly the pre-detection behaviour rather than failing closed on a live auth path.

Compatibility: `AuthConfig` gains a public `refresh_reuse_grace` field, so struct-literal construction must name it. `AuthAuditEvent` is now `#[non_exhaustive]`, so exhaustive matches need a wildcard arm. An immediate replay of a just-rotated token now returns 200 with the same pair instead of 401; callers asserting the old shape must expect the retry semantics. The semver report picks these up from the API itself, so the release moves the compatibility field.

* fix(auth): keep a committed rotation when its tombstone write fails

The refresh rotation is durable before the tombstone is written, so
returning the tombstone error withheld the only live refresh token from
its owner. Its retry with the spent token then found no tombstone and was

title: feat(backup)!: a backup is the whole agent, and restores between plain, hardened and TEE VTAs
body:
## Problem

- **A backup wasn't the whole agent.** Export collected six keyspaces by hand. Ten more listed in `BACKED_UP` were never exported: audit keys, consent, approvers, memory, room groups, room invitations, app state, persona, policy and task consent. The vault, DID templates and issued credentials were excluded as "known gaps".
- **A restore into a TEE VTA never took effect.**
  - Both import paths passed `store: None`, so the KMS re-seal never ran. The enclave rebooted into its *old* seed.
  - Even if the re-seal had run, the rows were written under the old seed-derived storage key.
  - The three KMS ciphertext rows were rewritten one at a time, so a crash between writes bricked the enclave.
  - The single-use Mode-B carve-out was left open on the restored VTA.
- **Cross-environment restores had further gaps.** The identity was written only to in-memory config, the enclave's own rows were carried to non-enclave VTAs, and the persona correlation index (keyed from the storage key) silently missed every lookup.

## Change

- **Export** walks `BACKED_UP` and dumps every row into the new `vta-backup-v2` format. The v2 envelope binds its metadata as AES-GCM associated data (AAD). The keyspace partition is now inclusion by default, with a stated reason for every exclusion. Rows tied to one deployment (`ENVIRONMENT_BOUND_ROWS`) stay behind and are re-created on the target. v1 backups still restore.
- **Import stages; boot applies.**
  - The payload is staged in `bootstrap`, sealed under a key derived from the *restored* seed.
  - The seed is committed through `RestoreCommitter`: the secret store, or one KMS-sealed row in an enclave.
  - The VTA then re-executes itself. Each binary applies a pending restore before anything else reads the store.
  - A crash before the commit leaves the VTA unchanged; a crash after it means the next boot applies the restore again.
- **TEE:** at commit, the restore reserves a version on the restored DID's anti-rollback counter. At boot, the integrity manifest is re-baselined only if the counter is still exactly at that version, so replaying a restore is refused. The carve-out is closed and the identity is written to the store.
- **Internal keys** are still never carried. Their records are, and the restore reports each one whose material is lost.
- **`--replace-identity`** (or `ext["org.openvtc"].replaceIdentity` on the Trust Task) is required to restore over a different running DID. Preview now checks this too.
- **VTI-VTA-051:** the restore writes a provenance record, adds a `backup.restore.applied` audit row, and `GET /health/details` reports `restored`.

Design note: `docs/05-design-notes/backup-restore-portability.md`. Operator guide: `docs/02-vta/backup-restore.md`.

## Tests

- `every_backed_up_keyspace_survives_a_round_trip`: export → stage → boot-apply across all 8 pairings of plain, hardened and TEE. Checks that every backed-up keyspace comes back and that nothing excluded or deployment-bound travels.
- Also covered:
  - staging crash consistency: an uncommitted stage is discarded, and applying twice is idempotent
  - refusing to apply on a different kind of deployment
  - internal keys are kept only on their own VTA
  - v1 backups still restore
  - identity replacement detaches hosted DIDs
  - a replayed restore is refused at the integrity re-baseline
  - persona indexes are rebuilt
  - payload validation refuses writes into `bootstrap` or `internal_keys`

Local runs:
- `cargo test --workspace --exclude vtc-service --exclude vtc-client --no-fail-fast` ✅
- `cargo test -p vtc-service -p vtc-client` ✅
- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings` ✅
- `cargo fmt --check` ✅

**Not exercised locally:** the real KMS calls (`seal_restored_secrets`, `adopt_restored_secrets`) and the DynamoDB counter reservation. The logic around them is unit-tested with mocks, but an end-to-end restore into a live Nitro enclave still needs a run.

feat(backup)!: a backup is the whole agent, and restores between plain, hardened and TEE VTAs (#1655)

A backup now carries every row of every keyspace in vta_keyspaces::BACKED_UP
(format vta-backup-v2) and restores into a plain, hardened or Nitro-enclave
VTA from any of them. VTI-VTA-001, VTI-VTA-050, VTI-VTA-051, VTI-KEY-033.

Fixed:

- Export collected six keyspaces by hand. Ten more listed in BACKED_UP
  (audit_key, consent, consent_approvers, memory, room_groups,
  room_invitations, app_state, persona, policy, task_consent) were never
  exported, and vault, did_templates and issued_credentials were excluded as
  known gaps. Export now walks BACKED_UP; a census test restores a row from
  every keyspace across all eight environment pairings.
- A restore into a TEE never took effect: the KMS re-seal ran only with a
  store both callers passed as None. It also wrote rows under the old
  seed-derived storage key, rewrote three KMS rows non-atomically, and left
  the Mode-B carve-out open.

Import no longer writes the live store. It stages the payload in bootstrap,
sealed under a key derived from the restored seed, commits that seed through
RestoreCommitter (the secret store, or one KMS-sealed row in an enclave), and
re-execs. Each binary applies a pending restore before anything else reads the
store. An import that dies before its commit changes nothing; one that dies
after it is applied on the next boot.

In an enclave, committing a restore reserves the restored DID's anti-rollback
counter, and boot re-baselines the integrity manifest only at that exact
version, so a replayed stage is refused. The carve-out is closed and the
identity is written to the store.

Internal keys are still never carried. Their records are, and preview, the
import result and the restore provenance name the ones that come back without
material.

Breaking:

- BackupPayload gains keyspaces, source_environment and
  internal_keys_not_carried. ImportRequest gains replace_identity.
  FinalizeImportBody gains ext.
- vta-backup: apply_import and BootstrapReEncryptor are replaced by
  stage_import, RestoreCommitter and restore::*. DescriptorDeps and
  export_backup take a BackupTarget.
- A backup of a DID other than the running one needs --replace-identity
  (ext["org.openvtc"].replaceIdentity on the Trust Task).
- Imports reboot the VTA instead of soft-restarting it.

VTI-VTA-051: the restore writes a provenance record, adds a
backup.restore.applied audit row, and GET /health/details reports restored.

title: feat(persona)!: wear a face here without naming a persona DID
body:
Implements trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf#589 (design note
persona-context-first.md §9.7).

binding/set takes an omitted `personaDid`, and profile/compose takes
`wear: true`: the agent uses the persona the holder already uses in the
context — the one DID with a binding record there, current or cleared —
and names it in the response. None is refused (`noPersonaHere`),
several are refused (`personaAmbiguous`, naming them), and compose
refuses `wear` beside a `personaDid` (`wearAndPersona`). Neither task
mints a persona: a DID has a lifecycle of its own, and a write that could
half-create one would leave a published identity nobody holds.

PersonaStore::persona_here answers one, none or several from the
context's binding records. A DID merely registered in a context does not
count: the agent's own DIDs and integrations live in contexts too.

`pnm persona binding set` takes an optional --persona-did; `pnm persona
profile compose --wear`. Takes trust-tasks-rs 0.21.17.

BREAKING: VtaClient::persona_binding_set takes `Option<&str>` for the
persona; PersonaBindingSetBody.persona_did is optional; ComposeRequest
gains `wear` and ComposeRefusal three variants; vta-cli-common
cmd_binding_set and cmd_profile_compose change.

title: feat(tui): make values from a community's own faces reusable
body:
The last piece of the promote flow in the TUI.

- **Communities tab, `f`** opens *Faces made for <community>*: each face made there, with the values it keeps to itself.
- **↑/↓** move between values; **space** chooses values within one face (a choice in another face replaces it — a promotion moves one face).
- **⏎** shows the one-way warning; a second **⏎** sends `persona/attribute/promote` with the face's version, so a concurrent edit is refused, not overwritten. Moving or changing the choice withdraws the question.

Core: `openvtc_core::persona::lifecycle::{local_faces, promote}`.

title: Trust Task Context Binding on published mechanisms, taskContext re-anchoring, and W3C proof/digest alignment
body:
Consolidated Working Draft 01 batch from the task force's working fork, superseding #15 by carrying it: the first commits are @bmiller59's #15 restructuring (authorship preserved), with three further changes built on top of it and the #15 first-pass review addressed. Closes #11. Resolves #17.

## What's inside, in order

**1. The #15 restructuring** (@bmiller59) — Trust Task Context Binding depends only on mechanisms already defined in the Trust Tasks core specification; the "qualifying specification" profile; outcome evidence travels with the presentation.

**2. `taskContext` re-anchoring and framework-0.4 alignment** — the outcome of trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf#173: `taskContext` carries the **`id` of the originating exchange's initiating document** (globally unique per the core specification's §4.3; the innermost exchange that attests the event, per §4.9.1), retiring the issuer-side uniqueness workaround. The qualifying profile is reworded against framework 0.4 (per-variant proof; the error variant honestly excluded — a task specification cannot strengthen `trust-task-error`'s own declaration; the no-`#response` escape hatch dropped). Outcome Interpretability cites the core specification's reply-disposition classification (§8.6) rather than hand-rolling the terminal/non-terminal split, and states the verifier's pairing checklist for retained evidence. A `trust-task-error` is failure evidence only, attributable to third parties when it carries `inResponseTo` (§8.2).

**3. W3C proof and digest alignment** (#17, all three items) — the VWC digest becomes `digestMultibase` (multibase multihash over the JCS canonical form the definition already named); multibase headers restricted to `z`/`u` per CID 1.0 §2.4 with alphabets enforced; proofs move from `Ed25519Signature2020` to the `DataIntegrityProof` envelope with `eddsa-jcs-2022` as the RECOMMENDED default suite (offline-verifiable; one canonicalization shared with `digestMultibase`) and `bbs-2023` named as the selective-disclosure path.

**4. The #15 first-pass review, addressed** — normative citations are commit-pinned permalinks (framework 0.4, `fbe196a`) so "pinned" is literally true; the stray subsection marking is removed; the per-issuer-uniqueness comment is mooted by the re-anchoring; and the term **"Trust Tasks core specification"** is now defined (`spec/terms-definitions/`), stating the core-vs-individual-specification architecture, explaining the upstream document's own "framework 0.4" version labels, and explicitly disclaiming the ToIP governance-framework sense.

## Evidence

The pairing checklist and the anchoring rule are executable: [`tsp-reference/ref-06w-witnessed-exchange`](https://github.com/berkmancenter/keyring-wallet/tree/doc/tsp-plan/tsp-reference/ref-06w-witnessed-exchange) runs the witnessed exchange end-to-end — the VWC's `taskContext` lands on the ceremony's initiating document `id` structurally, and the retained `submit#response` passes exactly the checks the text states. title: fix(persona)!: a credential-backed value follows its credential, and fails closed
body:
Credential-backed attributes were never resolved against their
credential: not at write (persona/attribute/put rule 3,
`credentialNotFound`) and, worse, not on read, where the Provenance
contract requires the maintainer to re-derive the value and fail closed
once the credential is revoked, expired, archived or deleted. A revoked
credential's value went on being presented.

vta-persona gains `derive`: a `CredentialSource` hook the service
implements over the vault, so the persona crate still does not depend
on it. The store asks it wherever a credential-backed value is about to
be believed:
- put: resolves the credential and takes its value (the supplied one is
  a display cache the spec lets the maintainer overwrite); one it cannot
  back is refused. `credential_refusal` gives the dispatcher the code.
- resolving a face (and so materialising a binding): the credential's
  current value, or nothing and `stale`.
- listing the pool: `stale` with `staleReason`, no value; a withheld
  value stays withheld.
- building a preview: re-derived from the context's copy, which carries
  the provenance; a withdrawn credential shows stale before approval.
- presenting: checked again, so a credential revoked between preview
  and present is not presented.
A pinned kept value is withheld too once its credential is withdrawn.

vta-vault `receive::stored_claims`: the claims a stored credential
carries — SD-JWT-VC re-verified against its issuer and reconstructed,
Data-Integrity read as stored, mdoc refused. vta-service's
`VaultCredentials` maps held/lifecycle/status/validity window/path to a
value or a StaleReason; attribute/put maps a refusal to
`persona/attribute/put:credentialNotFound`, and reads the stored value
back for its correlation count.

BREAKING: PersonaStore gains a field (and `with_credentials`); vta-persona
gains a module and an async-trait dependency.



Verified locally with the CI set: `cargo test --workspace --exclude vtc-service --exclude vtc-client` (4767 passed), `cargo test -p vtc-service -p vtc-client` (1810), clippy `-D warnings`, fmt.

title: Drop the informative credential categories; keep Edge Credentials as a class
body:
Implements the decision recorded in #28 (https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-cred-spec/issues/28#issuecomment-5696470196): drop the informative categories, keep Edge Credentials as a section and a defined term because it is a normative class rather than a category.

**Why edge stays and annotation goes.** A grouping earns a heading only if the specification says something about the group that it does not say about each member. Edge Verifiability, the VSC's profile-versus-type test, the `dtg:witnessed` profile and the VRC, VMC and VDC glossary entries all depend on the edge credential class. Nothing depended on the annotation category: its preamble was one sentence, its glossary entry said it annotates an edge, which was already untrue of the VSC, and its only other use was the VAC preamble explaining why the VAC was not in it.

**Changes**

- Abstract and Introduction list the seven types flat, with the VRC, VMC and VDC described as edge credentials that form a bi-directional pair. The "descriptive only" caveat goes.
- Taxonomy drops the mermaid diagram. Without the category nodes it duplicated the formal W3C type hierarchy printed directly beneath it, which never had categories.
- Edge Credentials preamble states the bilateral test once: an edge credential is one half of a pair whose relationship is only established when the counterparty issues the other half; every other credential is complete on the issuer's signature alone; a statement that would need the counterparty's agreement is an edge credential, not a VSC predicate profile.
- Annotation Credentials heading and its placement editor's note removed. VPC and VSC promoted to top-level sections in place, with the VSC's subsections promoted one level to match.
- VAC preamble loses the paragraph justifying its standalone placement and no longer contrasts itself with an annotation credential.
- Glossary: `DTG annotation credential` deleted. VPC and VSC entries become "a DTG credential that". `DTG credential` no longer lists three WD01 subtypes.
- `CONTEXT.md` updated to match.

**Not changed.** No schema, type string or `@context` change. `DTG edge credential` and the Edge Credentials section are unchanged apart from the added preamble paragraph. Every section still has either no subsections or more than one.

**Outline after this PR:** Edge Credentials (VRC, VMC, VDC, Edge Verifiability), VIC, VPC, VSC, VAC.

Closes #28.

title: Structural issues in categorization of DTG credentials
body:
In reviewing @martipos PR https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-cred-spec/pull/16, I realized we have an issue with spec as currently structured in Working Draft 01. 

We refer to "three functional categories" of DTG creds because at the proposal stage, we actually had three categories (with multiple members in each category). However, once we realized we only needed one verifiable invitation credential (VIC), we don't actually have three categories, only two:

1. Edge Credentials (VRCs and VMCs) 
2. Annotation Credentials (VWCs, VPCs, VECs)

Fixing this would also address the editorial issue that section "8. Invitation Credentials" currently only has just one subsection, "8.1. VIC (Verifiable Invitation Credential)". As a general rule, a spec should never have a section with only one subsection.

My proposed fix:

1. Move what is currently (in Working Draft 01) section "9. Annotation Credentials" to become the new section 8 (so it immediately follows section "7. Edge Credentials"). That way we cover the two categories of DTG credentials first in sections 7 and 8.
2. Change what is currently section "8. Invitation Credentials" to become the new section 9.
3. Change the name to "9. VIC (Verifiable Invitation Credential)".
4. Just include in section 9 the content of what is currently section 8.1.
